source: fa.wikisource.org — رباعیات خیام (تصحیح فروغی و غنی)

lines: برخیز بُتا بیار بهر دل ما
حلّ کن بجمال خویشتن مُشکلِ ما
یک کوزه شراب تا بهم نوش کنیم
زان پیش که کوزه‌ها کنند از گِلِ ما
quatrains.source_title: برخیز بتا بیار بهر دل ما
literal: Rise, my idol, and bring something for our hearts' sake;
By your beauty, unravel the knot we are caught in;
A single jug of wine, so we can drink together,
Before they shape jugs out of our own clay.
poetic: Rise, sweet idol; bring a cup to soothe the heart,
And with your beauty untangle the knot of mine.
One jug between us, let us drink while we can,
Before the potters knead our dust for wine.
quatrains.note: A classic Khayyam opener: the beloved (boot, literally idol) and wine against mortality. The pun lands in the closing line — we will be clay from which future jugs are made. The image threads through the whole Rubaiyat.

lines: چون عهده نمی‌شود کسی فردا را
حالی خوش دار این دل پُر سودا را
می نوش بماهتاب ای ماه که ماه
بسیار بِتابَد و نیابَد ما را
quatrains.source_title: چون عهده نمی‌شود کسی فردا را
literal: Since no one can vouch for tomorrow,
Keep this heart full of longing glad for now;
Drink wine by moonlight, O moon, for the moon
Will shine on and on and not find us here.
poetic: No one can stand surety for tomorrow,
So cheer this restless, longing heart today.
Drink in the moonlight, moon-faced one, for the moon
Will shine on many nights and find us gone.
quatrains.note: The triple play on maah (moon) — as heavenly body, as term of endearment for the beloved, and as month — is a signature Khayyam figure. The argument from impermanence to present joy is the Rubaiyat's core Epicurean move.

lines: قرآن که مهین کلام خوانند آنرا
گه‌گاه نه بر دوام خوانند آنرا
بر گِردِ پیاله آیتی هست مقیم
کاندر همه جا مدام خوانند آنرا
quatrains.source_title: قرآن که مهین کلام خوانند آنرا
literal: The Qur'an, called the greatest of words,
People read now and then, not continually;
But round the rim of the wine-cup a verse is inscribed
Which they read everywhere, always.
poetic: The Qur'an, called the Word of highest worth,
They open now and then, and then forget.
But round the winecup's lip a verse is etched
That every drinker reads, and reads again.
quatrains.note: A cheeky reversal of Muslim piety: the wine-cup, often engraved with verses or measurement lines, becomes the scripture actually read with devotion. The Persian mudaam plays on 'continually' and 'wine' (the root mudaam can denote both).

lines: گر می نخوری طعنه مزن مستانرا
بنیاد مکن تو حیله و دستانرا
تو غره بدان مشو که می می نخوری
صد لقمه خوری که می غلام است آنرا
quatrains.source_title: گر می نخوری طعنه مزن مستانرا
literal: If you do not drink, do not taunt the drunkards;
Do not build a foundation of trickery and deceit;
Do not be proud that you do not drink wine —
You swallow a hundred bites that wine is only a slave to.
poetic: If you don't drink, don't taunt the men who do,
And don't build palaces on lies and schemes.
Don't boast to me that wine has never passed your lips —
You swallow worse than anything wine could serve.
quatrains.note: Khayyam's perennial target: the sober moralist whose sins (gluttony, avarice, spite) dwarf the drunkard's. The line about wine as 'slave' to worse sins is especially biting.

lines: هرچند که رنگ و بوی زیباست مرا
چون لاله رخ و چو سرو بالاست مرا
معلوم نشد که در طربخانهٔ خاک
نقّاش ازل بهرچه آراست مرا
quatrains.source_title: هرچند که رنگ و بوی زیباست مرا
literal: Though I have color and fragrance and beauty,
A tulip cheek and cypress stature,
It remains unclear why, in this pleasure-house of dust,
The eternal Painter designed me at all.
poetic: Though I wear color, fragrance, and a face
Cheek like the tulip, tall as a cypress tree,
Still it is not made clear, in this dust-built hall of joy,
Why the eternal Painter fashioned me.
quatrains.note: Tarabkhana-ye khak (pleasure-house of dust) names the world as a brief revel in a cemetery. Naqqash-e azal, the Painter of Eternity, is the Neoplatonic-Sufi creator — and Khayyam, for all his sensual praise of his own body, still asks why.

lines: مائیم و می و مطرب و این کُنج خراب
جان و دل و جام و جابه پُر درد شراب
فارغ ز امید رحمت و بیم عذاب
آزد ز خاک و باد و از آتش و آب
quatrains.source_title: مائیم و می و مطرب و این کنج خراب
literal: Here we are: the wine, the musician, and this ruined corner;
Soul and heart and cup and robe all brimming with wine's lees;
Free from hope of mercy and fear of punishment,
Unbound from earth and wind and fire and water.
poetic: Just us: the wine, the minstrel, and this ruined nook,
Body and heart and cup and robe, all drenched in wine.
Done with the hope of mercy, done with fear of hell —
Past earth and air, past fire and water too.
quatrains.note: The 'ruined corner' (kunj-e kharab) is the rind's tavern — disreputable, outside orthodoxy. Rising above the four elements is a Sufi trope of union, twisted by Khayyam into bacchanalian release from both reward and damnation.

lines: آن قصر که جمشید در او جام گرفت
آهو بچه کرد و روبه آرام گرفت
بهرام که گور میگرفتی همه عمر
دیدی که چگونه گور بهرام گرفت
quatrains.source_title: آن قصر که جمشید در او جام گرفت
literal: The palace where Jamshid raised his cup
Now shelters fawns and gives foxes rest;
Bahram, who hunted the wild ass all his life —
See how the grave has hunted Bahram down.
poetic: The palace where Jamshid once raised his cup
Is den for the fox now, and the fawn's retreat.
Bahram, who hunted the onager all his years —
Look how the grave hunted him down to meet.
quatrains.note: Jamshid owned the legendary seven-ringed cup that mirrored the world; Bahram V 'the Wild Ass-Hunter' was the Sasanian king whose nickname Khayyam puns: gur means both onager and grave. FitzGerald built his famous 'Lion and Lizard' stanza on this.

lines: ابر آمد و باز بر سَرِ سبزه گریست
بی باده گُلرنگ نمی‌باید زیست
این سبزه که امروز تماشاگه ماست
تا سبزهٔ خاک ما تماشاگه کیست
quatrains.source_title: ابر آمد و باز بر سر سبزه گریست
literal: The cloud came, and wept again over the grass;
One cannot live without wine the color of roses.
This grass, which today is our meadow to gaze on —
Whose gazing-place will the grass over our dust be?
poetic: The cloud has come and wept upon the grass again;
Without the rose-red wine, no life is worth the breath.
This grass we loll and marvel at today —
Whose eyes will it refresh, grown from our dust?
quatrains.note: A spring rain lyric that turns to the grave in its fourth line. Tamashagah — 'a place to behold' — appears in lines 3 and 4 to frame the reversal: we look at the grass; one day others will look at the grass that is us.

lines: اکنون که گُلِ سعادتت پُربار است
دست تو ز جام می چرا بیکار است
می خور که زمانه دشمنی غدّار است
در یافتن روز چنین دشوار است
quatrains.source_title: اکنون که گل سعادتت پربار است
literal: Now that the rose of your good fortune is in full bloom,
Why is your hand empty of the wine-cup?
Drink wine, for time is a treacherous enemy;
Finding another day like this will be hard.
poetic: Now that fortune's rose is fully blown for you,
Why does your hand stay empty of the cup?
Drink — for time is a faithless enemy,
And such a day as this will not return.
quatrains.note: Zamana — 'the age, time, fortune' — is personified as a treacherous foe, a Khayyamian commonplace. The rose of happiness 'laden with fruit' in the original carries the Persian sense of fleeting, ripe-on-the-point-of-falling abundance.

lines: امروز تُرا دسترسِ فردا نیست
و اندیشهٔ فردات بجز سودا نیست
ضایع مکن ایندم اَر دِلَت شیدا نیست
کاین باقی عمر را بها پیدا نیست
quatrains.source_title: امروز ترا دسترس فردا نیست
literal: Today you have no grasp on tomorrow,
And thinking about tomorrow is nothing but delusion;
Do not waste this moment, if your heart is not mad,
For the price of the life remaining is not clear.
poetic: You have no hold on what tomorrow brings,
And thinking forward breeds no fruit but dread.
Waste not this moment, if your heart still beats —
Who knows the worth of the life that's left ahead?
quatrains.note: A sober didactic rubaʿi in contrast to the bacchanalian ones. Sowda in line 2 carries both 'melancholy' and 'futile obsession' — a technical Persian term for bile-driven mania.

lines: ای آمده از عالم روحانی تفت
حیران شده در پنج و چهار و شش و هفت
مِی خور چو ندانی از کجا آمدهٔ
خوش باش ندانی بکجا خواهی رفت
quatrains.source_title: ای آمده از عالم روحانی تفت
literal: You who came from the spiritual world in haste,
Bewildered among the five, the four, the six, and the seven,
Drink wine, since you do not know where you came from;
Be glad, since you do not know where you are going.
poetic: You who came pelting from the spirit-world,
Dazed among the five, four, six, and seven,
Drink wine: you do not know from where you came.
Be glad: you do not know toward what you're going.
quatrains.note: The numbers are the Aristotelian-Islamic cosmological furniture: five senses, four elements, six directions, seven planetary spheres. Against this scholastic scaffolding, Khayyam's answer is wine. FitzGerald echoes this in 'Into this Universe' (1st ed. XXIX, 5th ed. XXIX).

lines: ای چرخ فلک خرابی از کینهٔ تُست
بیدادگری شیوهٔ دیرینهٔ تُست
ای خاک اگر سینهٔ تو بشکافند
بس گوهر قیمتی که در سینهٔ تُست
quatrains.source_title: ای چرخ فلک خرابی از کینه تست
literal: O wheel of heaven, the ruin comes from your spite;
Injustice is your ancient way;
O earth, if they cleaved open your breast,
So many precious jewels would be found there.
poetic: Wheel of heaven, this ruin is your spite;
Oppression is your long, inherited craft.
And you, O earth — if they split your breast in two,
What hoard of priceless jewels they would find.
quatrains.note: The charkh-e falak (wheel of the firmament) is the Ptolemaic sky blamed for all misfortune. The second couplet turns to buried kings and beauties — the earth as a vault of wasted splendor, a theme FitzGerald picks up repeatedly.

lines: ای دل چو زمانه میکند غمناکت
ناگه برود ز تن روانِ پاکت
بر سبزه نشین و خوش بزی روزی چند
زان پیش که سبزه بردَمَد از خاکت
quatrains.source_title: ای دل چو زمانه میکند غمناکت
literal: O heart, since the age makes you sorrowful,
Suddenly your pure spirit will leave your body;
Sit on the grass and live well a few days,
Before the grass sprouts from your dust.
poetic: Heart, since the age is bent on grieving you,
And since your pure soul will depart, and soon,
Sit on the grass, enjoy these few days while you can —
Before the grass comes sprouting from your bones.
quatrains.note: The grass-to-grave image returns (see #8, #51). The injunction 'sit on the grass' (bar sabza neshin) is a common Persian call to the picnic and to acceptance of mortality in a single gesture.

lines: این بحر وجود آمده بیرون ز نهفت
کس نیست که این گوهر تحقیق بسُفت
هر کس سخنی از سَرِ سودا گفتند
زان روی که هست کس نمیداند گفت
quatrains.source_title: این بحر وجود آمده بیرون ز نهفت
literal: This sea of being has surfaced from the hidden;
No one has pierced this pearl of truth.
Everyone has spoken a word according to their own mania;
The face of what is, no one is able to speak.
poetic: This sea of being has risen up from hidden depths;
No one has ever pierced this pearl of truth.
Each has declared his theory out of his own delirium;
The face of what actually is, no one can say.
quatrains.note: Classical skeptical Khayyam: every metaphysical position is a private sawda (obsession, phantasm). The sea/pearl figure — truth as an unpierced pearl in the sea of existence — is standard Sufi idiom that Khayyam uses to negate Sufi claims.

lines: این کوزه چو من عاشق زاری بوده است
بند سرِ زُلف نگاری بوده است
این دسته که بر گَردنِ او می‌بینی
دستی است که بر گَردنِ یاری بوده است
quatrains.source_title: این کوزه چو من عاشق زاری بوده است
literal: This jug was once a longing lover like me;
It was entangled in the tresses of some beauty;
This handle you see fitted around its neck
Was once a hand around the neck of a beloved.
poetic: This jug, like me, once burned and longed and sighed,
Was caught in the dark tresses of some love.
The handle you see curling round its throat —
That was a hand, once, round a lover's throat.
quatrains.note: One of the most beloved Kuza-nama (Book of Pots) quatrains. The pot is built from the dust of a former lover, and its very handle remembers an embrace. FitzGerald's Book of Pots draws on this cluster of poems.

lines: این کوزه که آبخوارهٔ مُزدوریست
از دیدهٔ شاهیست و دل دستوریست
هر کاسهٔ می که بر کفِ مخموریست
از عارض مستی و لب مستوریست
quatrains.source_title: این کوزه که آبخواره مزدوریست
literal: This jug that is the water-bowl of a hired laborer
Is from the eye of a king and the heart of a minister;
Every cup of wine in a drunkard's palm
Is from a tipsy face and a veiled lip.
poetic: This jug the day-laborer drinks from at his work
Is built from a king's eye, a minister's heart.
Every wine-bowl the drunkard lifts to his mouth
Was once a flushed cheek, once a hidden lip.
quatrains.note: A variant of the 'clay once had names' topos. Note the social reversal — the common man drinks from what was royalty; universal leveling through death and recycled dust.

lines: این کهنه رباط را که عالم نامست
وارامگه ابلق صبح و شامست
بزمیست که واماندهٔ صد جمشید است
قصریست که تکیه‌گاه صد بهرامست
quatrains.source_title: این کهنه رباط را که عالم نامست
literal: This worn caravanserai called 'the world'
Is the resting-place of the piebald dawn and evening;
It is a feast, the leftovers of a hundred Jamshids;
It is a palace, the resting-place of a hundred Bahrams.
poetic: This battered inn we call the world
Is where the piebald horse of day and night comes in to rest.
A banquet — scraps from a hundred Jamshids left;
A palace — where a hundred Bahrams laid their heads.
quatrains.note: Kohna ribat (old caravanserai) is FitzGerald's 'batter'd Caravanserai' almost verbatim. The piebald dawn/evening is the black-and-white horse of time. A favorite Khayyamian emblem of impermanent lodging.

lines: این یک دو سه روزه نوبت عمر گذشت
چون آب بجویبار و چون باد بدشت
هرگز غم دو روز مرا یاد نگشت
روزی که نیامده است و روزی که گذشت
quatrains.source_title: این یک دو سه روزه نوبت عمر گذشت
literal: This turn of life, these one or two or three days, has passed
Like water in the brook, like wind in the desert;
Two days' grief has never come to my mind:
The day that has not come, and the day that has gone.
poetic: This turn of life — two days, three — has slipped past,
Like water in the brook, like wind across the plain.
Two days' worth of grief I never bear in mind:
The day not yet arrived, the day already gone.
quatrains.note: A cleaner statement of the Khayyamian 'no yesterday, no tomorrow' discipline. FitzGerald transposes this into 'Unborn To-Morrow and dead Yesterday' (FG 1st XXXVII, FG 5th LVII).

lines: بر چهرهٔ گل نسیم نوروز خوشست
در صحن چمن روی دل افروز خوشست
از دی که گذشت هرچه گوئی خوش نیست
خوش باش و ز دی مگو که امروز خوشست
quatrains.source_title: بر چهره گل نسیم نوروز خوشست
literal: The breeze of Nowruz on the rose's face is sweet;
In the garden's meadow, the heart-kindling face is sweet;
Whatever you say of yesterday, which has passed, is not sweet;
Be glad, and do not speak of yesterday, for today is sweet.
poetic: Nowruz's breath upon the rose is sweet;
In the green plot, the kindling face is sweet.
Whatever you say of yesterday is not sweet —
Be glad, speak not of yesterday: today is sweet.
quatrains.note: Nowruz is the Persian New Year (vernal equinox), a pre-Islamic festival Khayyam himself helped set on its correct solar date in the Jalali calendar reform. The refrain khush-ast threads the quatrain like a bell.

lines: پیش از من و تو لیل و نهاری بوده است
گردنده فلک نیز بکاری بوده است
هرجا که قدم نهی تو بر روی زمین
آن مَردُمَک چشم نگاری بوده است
quatrains.source_title: پیش از من و تو لیل و نهاری بوده است
literal: Before me and you, there have been many nights and days;
The turning firmament, too, was at its work.
Every step you take upon the earth —
That is the pupil of some beloved's eye.
poetic: Before us, nights and days in great succession;
The wheeling heavens, too, had their affairs.
Each step you take on this dust of ours —
Is the dark pupil of some lover's eye.
quatrains.note: The mardomak — literally 'little person,' the pupil — makes the point sharper: we walk on eyes that once saw us. Compare FitzGerald's 'Hyacinth' quatrain and its Persian source in #49.

lines: تا چند زنم بروی دریاها خشت
بیزار شدم ز بُت پرستان کِنِشت
خیّام که گفت دوزخی خواهد بود
کِه رفت بدوزخ و کِه آمد ز بهشت
quatrains.source_title: تا چند زنم بروی دریاها خشت
literal: How long shall I throw bricks upon the surface of seas?
I am sick of the idol-worshipers of the synagogue.
Who said Khayyam would be a dweller in hell?
Who has gone to hell, and who has come from heaven?
poetic: How long must I keep throwing bricks into the sea?
I'm sick of the idol-worshipers and their shrines.
Who says Khayyam will be a citizen of hell?
Who ever went to hell, or came back from paradise?
quatrains.note: 'Throwing bricks on the sea' is a Persian idiom for futile labor. Kinisht denotes the synagogue or any non-Muslim shrine; Khayyam's target is any creed that claims certain knowledge of damnation. No witness has returned from either realm.

lines: ترکیب پیالهٔ که در هم پیوست
بشکستن آن روا نمیدارد مست
چندین سر و پای نازنین از سر دست
بر مِهرِ که پیوست و بکین که شکست
quatrains.source_title: ترکیب پیاله که در هم پیوست
literal: The composition of the cup that was joined together —
A drunkard considers it wrong to break it;
So many lovely heads and hands and feet —
By whose love joined, and by whose spite broken?
poetic: The cup composed and fitted into shape —
A drunk man thinks it wrong to smash the thing.
So many lovely hands, feet, heads: whose love
Composed them? Whose resentment brought them down?
quatrains.note: A sharp theological jab: if even a drinker refuses to break his cup, why does the Maker break His human vessels? The problem of evil in miniature. Echoes Job's 'Thy hands have made me, yet thou destroyest me.'

lines: ترکیب طبایع چو بکام تو دَمی است
رو شاد بزی اگرچه بر تو ستمی است
با اهل خِرَد باش که اصل تَنِ تو
گَردیّ و نسیمی و غباریّ و دَمی است
quatrains.source_title: ترکیب طبایع چو بکام تو دمی است
literal: Since the compound of the elements is for a breath to your liking,
Go, live gladly, though it is a tyranny on you;
Be with the wise, for the root of your body
Is a speck, a breeze, a bit of dust, a breath.
poetic: Since the elements' mixture pleases you for a breath,
Go, live gladly, though it wrongs you in the end.
Keep company with the wise: your body's root
Is a speck, a breeze, a whirl of dust, a breath.
quatrains.note: The four elements reappear as the fleeting stuff we are made of. Tarkib-e tabayeʿ is the Aristotelian 'mixture of natures' (four humors, four elements) — a clinical framing that undercuts any claim to permanence.

lines: چون ابر بنوروز رخ لاله بشُست
برخیز و بجام باده کن عزم درست
کاین سبزه که امروز تماشاگه تُست
فردا همه از خاک تو برخواهد رست
quatrains.source_title: چون ابر بنوروز رخ لاله بشست
literal: When the cloud at Nowruz washed the tulip's face,
Rise, and set your mind firmly on the wine-cup;
For this grass, which today is your place of pleasure,
Tomorrow will all sprout from your dust.
poetic: When the Nowruz cloud washes the tulip's face,
Rise up — set your mind firmly on the cup.
For this green meadow you enjoy today
Tomorrow will sprout out of your dust.
quatrains.note: A close cousin to #8 and #13. Nowruz spring rain bathing the red tulip (khoon-e jigar — heart's blood — is the classical color) sets up the funereal turn. The tulip is the flower of martyrs in Persian poetry.

lines: چون بلبل مست راه در بُستان یافت
روی گُل و جام باده را خندان یافت
آمد بزبان حال در گوشم گفت
دریاب که عمر رفته را نتوان یافت
quatrains.source_title: چون بلبل مست راه در بستان یافت
literal: When the drunken nightingale found its way into the garden,
Found the face of the rose and the wine-cup laughing,
It came and in the language of its state, whispered in my ear:
'Seize the day — a life gone cannot be recovered.'
poetic: When the drunken nightingale gained the garden,
Saw the rose laughing and the cup beside it laugh,
It drew near and murmured in my ear:
'Hold the hour — lost life never comes back.'
quatrains.note: The Nightingale-and-Rose (bolbol o gol) is the great Persian love emblem. The intoxicated nightingale is a Sufi figure for the soul in rapture; Khayyam has it deliver a plain Epicurean message.

lines: چون چرخ بکام یک خردمند نگشت
تو خواه فلک هفت شُمر خواهی هشت
چون باید مُرد و آرزوها همه هشت
چه مور خورد بگور و چه گرگ بدشت
quatrains.source_title: چون چرخ بکام یک خردمند نگشت
literal: Since the wheel never turned to a wise man's liking,
Count the heavens as seven or eight, as you please;
Since we must die and leave all our wishes behind,
What matter whether the ant in the grave or the wolf in the field eats us?
poetic: Since the wheel never turned to please the wise,
Call the heavens seven, or eight — it's all the same.
Since we must die and leave each wish behind,
What matter ant in grave, or wolf in field, devours us?
quatrains.note: A deliberate shrug at the astronomical fine-tuning Khayyam himself practiced. 'Seven or eight heavens' is the debated Ptolemaic count; it doesn't matter, because the end is the same grave.

lines: چون لاله بنوروز قدح گیر بدست
با لاله رخی اگر ترا فرصت هست
می نوش بخرّمی که این چرخ کهن
ناگاه ترا چو خاک گرداند پست
quatrains.source_title: چون لاله بنوروز قدح گیر بدست
literal: Like the tulip at Nowruz, take the cup in hand;
With a tulip-cheeked one, if the chance is yours;
Drink wine with joy, for this old wheel
Will suddenly lay you low as dust.
poetic: Like the tulip at Nowruz, take up the cup,
With a tulip-cheeked companion, if you can.
Drink wine with joy, for this old circling wheel
Will cast you down to dust before you know.
quatrains.note: The tulip-cup analogy (the tulip's open red bloom resembling a raised wine-bowl) is a stock Persian image, deployed here as a call to imitate the flower while still whole.

lines: چون نیست حقیقت و یقین اندر دست
نتوان بامید شک همه عمر نشست
هان تا ننهیم جام می از کفِ دست
در بیخبری مرو چه هشیار و چه مست
quatrains.source_title: چون نیست حقیقت و یقین اندر دست
literal: Since truth and certainty are not in our hands,
We cannot sit a whole life hoping in doubt;
Beware: let us not let the wine-cup fall from our hands;
Whether drunk or sober, do not walk in ignorance.
poetic: Since truth and certainty are not in our grasp,
We cannot spend our lives hoping on doubt.
Take care — don't let the wine-cup leave your hand;
Drunk or sober, do not walk in the dark.
quatrains.note: A precise epistemological argument for drink: since we will never close the gap between doubt and certainty, waiting is wasted. Bikhabari — 'unknowing, obliviousness' — also puns on the bikhabar drunkenness of the later line.

lines: چون نیست ز هرچه هست جز باد بدست
چون هست بهرچه هست نقصان و شکست
انگار که هرچه هست در عالم نیست
پندار که هرچه نیست در عالم هست
quatrains.source_title: چون نیست ز هرچه هست جز باد بدست
literal: Since of all that is, nothing is left in hand but wind;
Since of all that is, there is deficiency and breakage;
Imagine that everything that is in the world is not;
Suppose that everything that is not in the world is.
poetic: Since of all that is, nothing remains in our hand but wind;
Since every thing that is carries its breakage in it —
Suppose that all there is in the world is not;
Imagine that all that is not in the world is.
quatrains.note: Pure ontology in four lines: being and non-being are interchangeable under the regime of impermanence. An echo of Pyrrhonist skepticism filtered through Islamic kalam.

lines: خاکی که بزیر پای هر نادانی است
کفّ صنمی و چهرهٔ جانانی است
هر خشت که بر کنگرهٔ ایوانی است
انگشت وزیر یا سَرِ سلطانی است
quatrains.source_title: خاکی که بزیر پای هر نادانی است
literal: The dust under the foot of every ignorant man
Is the palm of some idol and the face of some beloved;
Every brick on the cornice of a palace
Is the finger of a minister or the head of a sultan.
poetic: The dust beneath some idler's trampling foot
Is the palm of an idol, the face of a loved one.
Every brick set in the battlement of a palace
Is the finger of a minister, the head of a king.
quatrains.note: A kindred poem to #20 and #49. The conceit that built walls are made of bones is medieval commonplace; Khayyam sharpens it with the walking-on-idols-and-beloveds image in the first couplet.

lines: دارنده چو ترکیب طبایع آراست
از بهر چه افکندش اندر کم و کاست
گر نیک آمد شکستن از بهر چه بود
ور نیک نیامد این صُوَر عیب کراست
quatrains.source_title: دارنده چو ترکیب طبایع آراست
literal: Since the Possessor composed the mixture of natures,
Why did He cast it into deficiency and ruin?
If it came out well, why is it broken?
And if it did not come out well, whose fault is the form?
poetic: If the Creator composed the mixture of our natures,
Why cast it into flaw and breakage, then?
If it came out well — why break the vessel?
If it came out badly — whose fault is that form?
quatrains.note: The forensic version of #22, now aimed directly at divine justice. If the work is good, why destroy it? If it is bad, the Craftsman is at fault either way. Echoes the classical Epicurean trilemma.

lines: در پردهٔ اسرار کسی را ره نیست
زین تعبیه جان هیچ کس آگه نیست
جز در دل خاک هیچ منزلگه نیست
میْ خور که چنین فسانه‌ها کوته نیست
quatrains.source_title: در پرده اسرار کسی را ره نیست
literal: No one has a path to the curtain of secrets;
No soul is aware of this hidden arrangement;
There is no lodging-place except in the heart of the dust;
Drink wine, for such fables are not short.
poetic: No one finds the way behind the curtain of secrets;
No soul knows the arrangement of this mystery.
No lodging awaits us but the heart of the dust —
Drink wine: the fables are long, and we are brief.
quatrains.note: Parda-ye asrar (curtain of secrets) is a Sufi technical phrase that Khayyam appropriates to deny what Sufis claim: no one passes it. FitzGerald's 'Veil past which I could not see' (FG 1st XXXII) draws on this family.

lines: در خواب بدم مرا خردمندی گفت
کز خواب کسی را گُلِ شادی نشکفت
کاری چکنی که با اجل باشد جُفت
میْ خور که بزیر خاک میباید خفت
quatrains.source_title: در خواب بدم مرا خردمندی گفت
literal: I was asleep, and a wise man said to me:
'No one's flower of joy has blossomed in sleep;
Why do you do a thing that is twin to death?
Drink wine, for you will sleep plenty under the dust.'
poetic: A wise man came to me while I lay asleep and said:
'No rose of joy was ever opened in sleep.
Why busy yourself with sleep, the twin of death?
Drink wine: you'll sleep long enough beneath the dust.'
quatrains.note: The sage-in-a-dream is a standard rubaʿi device. The Greek commonplace 'sleep is the brother of death' (Homer's kasignetos thanatoio) arrives via Arabic philosophical literature.

lines: در دایرهٔ که آمد و رفتن ماست
او را نه بدایت نه نهایت پیداست
کس می نزند دمی در این معنی راست
کاین آمدن از کجا و رفتن بکجاست
quatrains.source_title: در دایره که آمد و رفتن ماست
literal: In the circle in which our coming and going are,
Neither beginning nor end is evident.
No one speaks truly a moment on this meaning:
Where this coming is from, and where this going is to.
poetic: In the circle of our coming and our going,
Neither the start nor ending is in sight.
No one has spoken one true word on this —
Where the coming comes from, where the going goes.
quatrains.note: A key Khayyamian poem. FitzGerald's 'Into this Universe, and why not knowing, / Nor whence' (1st XXIX, 5th XXIX) is a fairly close descendant of this argument, though fused with related quatrains.

lines: در فصل بهار اگر بُتی حور سرشت
یک ساغر می دهد مرا بر لبِ کشت
هرچند بنزد عامه این باشد زشت
سگ به ز من اگر برم نام بهشت
quatrains.source_title: در فصل بهار اگر بتی حور سرشت
literal: In spring, if an idol of houri-nature
Gives me a bowl of wine on the edge of the sown field,
Though to the common people this may seem ugly,
A dog is better than I, if I mention paradise.
poetic: If in the spring, some houri-natured beauty
Hands me a cup of wine at the field's edge,
Though the crowd cry scandal — may a dog be better
Than I, if I so much as name the paradise to come.
quatrains.note: Khayyam swears against the very mention of behesht (paradise) in favor of the present garden. The self-curse ('a dog is better than I') is a rhetorical flourish common in rubaʿiyat and later Hafez.

lines: دَریاب که از روح جدا خواهی رفت
در پردهٔ اسرار فنا خواهی رفت
می نوش ندانی از کجا آمدهٔ
خوش باش ندانی بکجا خواهی رفت
quatrains.source_title: دریاب که از روح جدا خواهی رفت
literal: Know that you will depart, separated from your soul;
You will pass behind the curtain of the secrets of annihilation;
Drink wine — you do not know where you came from;
Be glad — you do not know where you are going.
poetic: Know this: you will depart, torn from your soul;
You will pass behind the veil of annihilation.
Drink wine: you don't know where you came from.
Be glad: you don't know where you're going.
quatrains.note: A near-duplicate of #11, differing in the opening line. The formula 'drink — be glad — you don't know' is a Khayyamian refrain. Multiple classical manuscripts preserve both versions.

lines: ساقی گُل و سبزه طربناک شده است
دریاب که هفتهٔ دگر خاک شده است
می نوش و گُلی بچین که تا درنگری
گل خاک شده است و سبزه خاشاک شده است
quatrains.source_title: ساقی گل و سبزه طربناک شده است
literal: Saki, the flowers and grass have grown joyful;
Seize them, for next week they will be dust.
Drink wine and pluck a rose, for by the time you look —
The rose has turned to dust, the grass to debris.
poetic: Saki — the flowers and the grass are glad;
Seize them: in a week they will be dust.
Drink wine and pick a rose. By the next glance
The rose is dust, the grass already straw.
quatrains.note: The Saki (cup-bearer) is addressed as audience and assistant to the carpe-diem injunction. Notice the brutal compression: 'one week' for the whole cycle of bloom and decay.

lines: عمری است مرا تیره و کاریست نه راست
محنت همه افزوده و راحت کم و کاست
شکر ایزد را که آنچه اسباب بلاست
ما را ز کس دگر نمی‌باید خواست
quatrains.source_title: عمری است مرا تیره و کاریست نه راست
literal: My life has been dark, and my business has gone crooked;
All grief multiplied, and comfort diminished;
Thanks be to God — all that is the apparatus of misfortune,
We never had to ask from anyone else.
poetic: My life's been dark, my work all gone awry;
Grief piled higher, every comfort lost.
Praise God — whatever misfortune's gear there is,
We've never had to go ask anyone else for it.
quatrains.note: One of Khayyam's bitter-comic quatrains. The mock-thanks ('we had to ask no one') reverses a pious formula — usually one thanks God for not depending on people. Here the joke is that misfortune has been abundant enough.

lines: فصلِ گُل و طرف جویبار و لبِ کشت
با یک دو سه اهل و لعبتی حور سرشت
پیش آر قدح که باده نوشان صبوح
آسوده ز مسجدند و فارغ ز کِنِشت
quatrains.source_title: فصل گل و طرف جویبار و لب کشت
literal: The season of flowers, the edge of the brook, the field's rim,
A few of the right people, and a houri-natured plaything;
Bring the cup — for those who drink the morning draught
Are untroubled by mosque and free of synagogue.
poetic: The season of the rose, the brook's green edge, the sown field's rim,
A friend or two, one houri-natured playmate,
Bring the cup — morning drinkers have no worry
For the mosque, and no part in the synagogue.
quatrains.note: The morning-drinker (nooshan-e sabooh) is the rind, the dawn-drinking libertine-saint of Persian poetry. To be 'free of mosque and synagogue' means free of institutional religion in all its forms.

lines: گر شاخ بقا ز بیخ بختت رست است
ور بر تن تو عمر لباسی چست است
در خیمهٔ تن که سایه‌بانی است ترا
هان تکیه مکن که چار میخش سست است
quatrains.source_title: گر شاخ بقا ز بیخ بختت رست است
literal: If the branch of permanence has sprouted from the root of your fortune,
And if life is a close-fitting garment on your body,
In the tent of the body, which is your canopy,
Beware — do not lean: its four pegs are loose.
poetic: If permanence has sprung from the roots of your fortune,
If life fits close upon you like a tailored robe,
Remember — in the body-tent that shelters you,
Four pegs are loose. Lean gently or not at all.
quatrains.note: The body-as-tent image, going back to Arabic qasida and to Indo-Iranian nomad life. The 'four pegs' stand for the four elements — pull any and the whole structure drops. Whinfield's #82 is the same tent-pitcher death figure.

lines: گویند کسان بهشت با حور خوش است
من میگویم که آب انگور خوش است
این نقد بگیر و دست از آن نسیه بدار
کآواز دهل شنیدن از دور خوش است
quatrains.source_title: گویند کسان بهشت با حور خوش است
literal: People say paradise with its houris is sweet;
I say the juice of the grape is sweet.
Take this cash in hand and let the credit go;
The sound of the drum is sweet from far away.
poetic: They say paradise is sweet, with its houris there.
I say: the juice of the grape is the sweet I know.
Take the cash in hand, let the credit go —
The drum is only sweet when it's far away.
quatrains.note: FitzGerald's famous 'Take the Cash in hand and waive the Rest; Oh, the brave Music of a distant Drum!' (1st XII, 5th XIII) is a close translation of this very quatrain. A textbook strong match.

lines: گویند مرا که دوزخی باشد مست
قولی است خلاف و دل در آن نتوان بست
گر عاشق و میخواره بدوزخ باشند
فردا بینی بهشت همچون کف دست
quatrains.source_title: گویند مرا که دوزخی باشد مست
literal: They tell me a drunkard will be a hell-dweller;
It is a false saying, the heart cannot rest on it.
If lovers and wine-drinkers are to be in hell,
You will see paradise tomorrow empty as the palm of your hand.
poetic: They tell me any drinker ends up in hell;
A false doctrine, no heart can rest on that.
If lovers and wine-drinkers are all damned,
Tomorrow paradise will be empty as an open palm.
quatrains.note: The 'palm of your hand' metaphor for emptiness is a Persian commonplace. Khayyam's argument is characteristically consequentialist: if the rule damns everyone warm-blooded, heaven becomes deserted.

lines: من هیچ ندانم که مرا آنکه سرشت
از اهل بهشت کرد یا دوزخ زشت
جامی و بتیّ و بربطی بر لبِ کشت
این هرسه مرا نقد و ترا نسیه بهشت
quatrains.source_title: من هیچ ندانم که مرا آنکه سرشت
literal: I do not know at all whether the One who shaped me
Made me of the people of paradise or of ugly hell;
A cup, an idol, and a lute at the field's edge —
All three for me are cash; paradise for you is credit.
poetic: I have no idea if the One who shaped me
Set me among the blessed, or the damned.
A cup, a beloved, a lute at the meadow's edge —
These three are cash for me; your paradise, a credit slip.
quatrains.note: The cash/credit opposition (naqd/nasyeh) returns from #41. The bot (idol/beloved) and barbat (a short-necked lute) alongside the wine-cup form Khayyam's preferred trinity.

lines: مهتاب بنور دامن شب بشکافت
می نوش دمی بهتر از این نتوان یافت
خوش باش و میندیش که مهتاب بسی
اندر سَرِ خاکِ یک بیک خواهد تافت
quatrains.source_title: مهتاب بنور دامن شب بشکافت
literal: The moonlight tore the hem of night with its light;
Drink a moment — you cannot find one better than this.
Be glad, do not worry, for the moon will shine many times
Over the dust of each of us, one by one.
poetic: The moon has torn the hem of the night with light;
Drink this instant — you'll find none better than now.
Be glad, unworried: the moon will shine many times
Over our dust, one by one, after we're gone.
quatrains.note: The moon theme from #2 returns — a long-lived cosmic witness to short human lives. FitzGerald's 'Yon rising Moon that looks for us again' (5th C) belongs to this emotional family.

lines: می خوردن و شاد بودن آئین من است
فارغ بودن ز کفر و دین دین من است
گفتم بعروس دهر کابین تو چیست
گفت دلِ خرّم تو کابین من است
quatrains.source_title: می خوردن و شاد بودن آئین من است
literal: Drinking wine and being glad is my custom;
Being free of unbelief and religion is my religion.
I said to the bride of the world: what is your dowry?
She said: a glad heart is my dowry.
poetic: To drink and be glad — that is my way;
Free of belief and unbelief — that is my creed.
I asked the bride of the world, 'What is your dowry?'
She said, 'A glad heart — that's all I ask.'
quatrains.note: The 'bride of the age' (aroos-e dahr) is a standard personification. Her dowry-demand, a glad heart, makes joy the only religious observance the world itself requires. A memorable anti-dogmatic couplet.

lines: می لعل مُذاب است و صراحی کان است
جسم است پیاله و شرابش جان است
آن جام بلورین که ز می خندان است
اشکی است که خون دل در او پنهان است
quatrains.source_title: می لعل مذاب است و صراحی کان است
literal: Wine is molten ruby, and the flask is its mine;
The body is the cup, and its wine is the soul.
The crystal cup that laughs with wine
Is a tear in which the heart's blood is hidden.
poetic: Wine is ruby melted; the flask, the mine;
The body is the cup, and the wine, the soul.
That crystal cup you see laughing with its wine —
Is a tear hiding the heart's own blood inside.
quatrains.note: One of the most intricate wine-poems in the corpus, built as nested metaphors (wine = ruby, flask = mine, body = cup, soul = wine, cup = tear, wine = blood). A bravura of the equivalential aesthetic.

lines: می نوش که عمر جاودانی این است
خود حاصلت از دور جوانی این است
هنگام گُل و باده و یاران سرمست
خوش باش دَمی که زندگانی این است
quatrains.source_title: می نوش که عمر جاودانی این است
literal: Drink wine, for eternal life is this;
Your portion from the round of youth is this;
The time of flowers, wine, and drunken friends —
Be glad for a moment, for life is this.
poetic: Drink — for eternal life is only this;
Your whole portion of youth, only this.
The hour of roses, wine, and drunken friends —
Be glad a moment. Life is only this.
quatrains.note: The refrain 'this is' (ain ast) anchors the argument: life is precisely, no more than, the present moment of companionship and drink. FitzGerald distils this into 'The Bird of Time has but a little way to fly' (1st VII, 5th VII) — adapted.

lines: نیکی و بدی که در نهادِ بشر است
شادی و غمی که در قضا و قدر است
با چرخ مکل حواله کاندر رَهِ عقل
چرخ از تو هزار بار بیچاره‌تر است
quatrains.source_title: نیکی و بدی که در نهاد بشر است
literal: The good and evil that are in human nature,
The joy and grief that are in fate and decree —
Do not assign them to the wheel, for on the path of reason
The wheel is a thousand times more helpless than you.
poetic: The good and the evil that are human nature,
The joy and grief lodged in fate and decree —
Don't lay them to the wheel: on reason's path,
The wheel is a thousand times more helpless than you.
quatrains.note: A striking inversion of the usual 'blame the heavens' plaint: the heavens are themselves mere machinery. The locus of responsibility falls back on human nature. A rare defense of agency in the corpus.

lines: در هر دشتی که لاله‌زاری بوده است
از سرخی خون شهریاری بوده است
هر شاخ بنفشه کز زمین میروید
خالی است که بر رخ نگاری بوده است
quatrains.source_title: در هر دشتی که لاله‌زاری بوده است
literal: In every desert where a tulip-bed has grown,
It is from the red blood of a prince;
Every stalk of violet that rises from the ground
Is a mole that was on the cheek of a beloved.
poetic: Wherever a tulip-bed has grown in the desert,
It has sprung from the red blood of some prince.
Every violet stalk rising from the earth
Was a mole on the cheek of someone's lover.
quatrains.note: The ancestor of FitzGerald's 'I sometimes think that never blows so red / The Rose as where some buried Caesar bled; / That every Hyacinth...from some once lovely Head' (1st XVIII, 5th XIX). A demonstrably strong match.

lines: هر ذرّه که در خاک زمینی بوده است
پیش از من و تو تاج و نگینی بوده است
گرد از رخ نازنین بآزرم فشان
کانهم رخ خوب نازنینی بوده است
quatrains.source_title: هر ذره که در خاک زمینی بوده است
literal: Every particle that has been in the dust of a land
Before me and you was a crown and signet-gem;
Brush the dust from that fine cheek gently,
For that too was the fine cheek of a beloved.
poetic: Every mote that lies in the dust of the earth
Was once a crown, or a signet stone, long before us.
Wipe the dust from that fair face with care —
That, too, was once the fine cheek of a loved one.
quatrains.note: A companion to #20, #30, and #49. The specific turn — 'wipe the dust gently' — gives this poem an unusual tenderness. FitzGerald's 'Ah, lean upon it lightly!' (from #51) is the nearest English analogue.

lines: هر سبزه که بر کنار جوئی رسته است
گوئی ز لب فرشته خوئی رسته است
پا بر سر سبزه تا بخواری ننهی
کان سبزه ز خاک لاله‌روئی رسته است
quatrains.source_title: هر سبزه که بر کنار جوئی رسته است
literal: Every blade of grass that has grown on the bank of a stream
It is as though it sprouted from the lip of an angel-natured one;
Do not set your foot on the grass with contempt,
For that grass has grown from the dust of a tulip-cheeked one.
poetic: Every blade of grass along the brook
Has sprung, you might say, from an angel's lip.
Do not tread it in contempt — remember,
That grass rose from the dust of a tulip-cheek.
quatrains.note: Source for FitzGerald's 'And this delightful Herb whose tender Green / Fledges the River's Lip on which we lean— / Ah, lean upon it lightly!' (1st XIX, 5th XX). The resemblance is line-for-line.

lines: یک جرعهٔ می ز ملک کاوس بهست
از تخت قباد و ملکت طوس بهست
هر ناله که رندی بسحرگاه زند
از طاعت زاهدان سالوس بهست
quatrains.source_title: یک جرعه می ز ملک کاوس بهست
literal: A sip of wine is better than the kingdom of Kavus;
It is better than the throne of Qubad and the realm of Tus;
Every moan that a libertine heaves at dawn
Is better than the worship of the hypocritical ascetics.
poetic: A single sip of wine beats Kavus's kingdom,
Is worth more than Qubad's throne, or the realm of Tus.
Every drunken sigh a libertine heaves at dawn
Outweighs the prayers of all the hypocrite ascetics.
quatrains.note: Kavus, Qubad, Tus — legendary Iranian kings and royal seats. Zahedan-e saloos is a sharp compound: 'hypocritical ascetics.' FitzGerald's 'Whose Throne of Saturn' and 'Throne of Kobad' (1st IX, 5th X) derive partly from this cluster.

lines: چون عمر بسر رسد چه شیرین و چه تلخ
پیمانه چو پُر شد چه بغداد و چه بلخ
می نوش که بعد از من و تو ماه بسی
از سلخ بغرّه آید از غرّه بسلخ
quatrains.source_title: چون عمر بسر رسد چه شیرین و چه تلخ
literal: When life ends, what matter if sweet or bitter?
When the cup is full, what matter if Baghdad or Balkh?
Drink wine, for after me and you, the moon will many times
Pass from the last night to the new, from the new night to the last.
poetic: When life runs out, what matter sweet or bitter?
When the cup is full, what matter Baghdad, Balkh?
Drink wine — the moon, long after us, will pass
From the month's last night to the new, and back.
quatrains.note: The sliding-between-months figure (salkh to ghorra) names the day the crescent disappears and the day it reappears: complete indifference at the lunar level to human lives. FitzGerald's 'Whether at Naishapur or Babylon' (5th VIII) is kin.

lines: انانکه محیط فضل و آداب شدند
در جمع کمال شمع اصحاب شدند
ره زین شب تاریک نبردند برون
گفتند فسانه و در خواب شدند
quatrains.source_title: انانکه محیط فضل و آداب شدند
literal: Those who became encompassing in excellence and manners,
Who in perfection became the candle of their companions —
They did not find a way out of this dark night either;
They told a fable and went to sleep.
poetic: Those who encompassed all excellence and manner,
Who in perfection were candles to their friends,
Even they found no way out of this dark night —
They told a fable, and then they went to sleep.
quatrains.note: 'They told a fable and went to sleep' is a devastating four-word summary of scholarly tradition. FitzGerald's 'The Revelations of Devout and Learn'd' (5th LXV) reworks the same idea: prophets as dreamers who went back to sleep.

lines: آنرا که بصحرای علل تاخته‌اند
بی او همه کارها بپرداخته‌اند
امروز بهانهٔ در انداخته‌اند
فردا همه آن بود که درساخته‌اند
quatrains.source_title: آنرا که بصحرای علل تاخته‌اند
literal: Those who have been driven to the desert of causes,
Without them, have completed all their work;
Today they have cast an excuse into it;
Tomorrow all will be as they have arranged.
poetic: Those hurried off into the desert of causes —
Without their say, the work is all done.
Today they toss in an excuse, a pretext;
Tomorrow all will be as ordained in advance.
quatrains.note: An argument against libertarian free will. Sahra-ye ʿelal is 'the desert/field of causes' — the Avicennan chain of causation. Human beings are rushed through it, and their will is backfilled as excuse.

lines: آنها که کهن شدند و اینها که نوند
هرکس بمراد خویش یک تک بدوند
این کهنه جهان بکس نماند باقی
رفتند و رویم و دیگر آیند و روند
quatrains.source_title: آنها که کهن شدند و اینها که نوند
literal: Those who have grown old and those who are new,
Everyone runs one dash toward their own desire;
This old world will last with no one;
They went, we go, and others come and go.
poetic: Those who have grown old, and those now new —
Each runs one sprint toward what he wants.
This old world will not linger with anyone:
They went, we go, others will come and go.
quatrains.note: The refrain-like 'raftand / ravim / ayand / ravand' (they went, we go, they come, they go) mimics the treadmill of generations in four Persian verbs.

lines: آنکس که زمین و چرخ و افلاک نهاد
بس داغ که او بر دل غمناک نهاد
بسیار لب چو لعل و زلفین چو مشک
در طبل زمین و حقهٔ خاک نهاد
quatrains.source_title: آنکس که زمین و چرخ و افلاک نهاد
literal: The One who set down earth, heaven, and the firmaments,
Set down many scars on the sorrowful heart;
Many lips like rubies and locks like musk
He set down in the drum of the earth and the casket of dust.
poetic: The One who laid out earth, sky, and the firmaments
Laid down many a scar upon the grieving heart.
Many a ruby lip and musky tress
He tucked into earth's drum and the casket of dust.
quatrains.note: Tabl-e zamin (drum of the earth) and hoqqe-ye khak (dust's casket) are vessels that contain all beauty past. The creator here is indicted for the destruction as much as for the creation.

lines: آرند یکی و دیگری بربایند
بر هیچ کسی راز همی نگشایند
ما را ز قضا جز این قدر ننمایند
پیمانهٔ عمر ماست می‌پیمایند
quatrains.source_title: آرند یکی و دیگری بربایند
literal: They bring one, and another they snatch away;
They do not unfold the secret to anyone;
They show us no more than this much of destiny:
Our cup is life — they are measuring.
poetic: They bring one in, and snatch away another;
The secret — they unveil it to no one.
Of destiny they show us only this:
Our cup is life — and they are measuring.
quatrains.note: A haunting, compressed lyric. The peymaneh pun works at two levels: a 'measure' of wine, and 'the measure of our days' — with the verb mipeymayand 'they are measuring' / 'they are pouring.'

lines: اجرام که ساکنان این ایوانند
اسباب تردُّدِ خردمندانند
هان تا سرِ رشتهٔ خِرَد گُم نکنی
کانانکه مدبّرند سرگردانند
quatrains.source_title: اجرام که ساکنان این ایوانند
literal: The heavenly bodies, dwellers of this hall,
Are the cause of confusion for wise men;
Beware — do not lose the thread of reason,
For those who govern are themselves in a daze.
poetic: The heavenly bodies, dwellers of this hall,
Are what confuse the clearest-sighted sage.
Beware — do not let reason's thread escape you,
For even those in charge are themselves adrift.
quatrains.note: A quietly radical line: the 'governors' of the universe (whether stars or angelic intelligences) are sargardan, 'reeling, lost.' Khayyam the astronomer writing against astrology. FitzGerald's 'Up from Earth's Centre' (1st XXXI, 5th XXXI) picks up the same skeptical register.

lines: از آمدنم نبود گردون را سود
وز رفتن من جلال و جاهش نفُزود
وز هیچ کسی نیز دو گوشم نشنود
کاین آمدن و رفتنم از بهر چه بود
quatrains.source_title: از آمدنم نبود گردون را سود
literal: My coming brought no gain to the firmament;
My going did not increase its glory or rank;
Nor did my two ears hear from anyone at all
Why this coming and going of mine has been.
poetic: My coming brought the firmament no gain,
My going added nothing to its state.
Nor have my two ears ever heard from anyone
Why this coming and going of mine has been.
quatrains.note: A bare, desolate statement of Khayyam's central question. The Persian has a near-metronomic parallelism. Voltaire's poem on the Lisbon earthquake contains similar lines — noted by Whinfield. An enduring lyric of existential unmooring.

lines: از رنج کشیدن آدمی حُرّ گردد
قطره چو کشد حبس صدف دُر گردد
گر مال نماند سر بماناد بجای
پیمانه چو شد تُهی دِگر پُر گردد
quatrains.source_title: از رنج کشیدن آدمی حر گردد
literal: Through enduring suffering a person becomes free.
When a drop accepts the shell's confinement, it becomes a pearl.
If wealth remains no more, may the head at least stay in its place.
When a cup is emptied, it will be filled again.
poetic: Suffering is what sets a person free;
the drop turns pearl inside captivity.
Let wealth go, so long as the head remains;
the cup drained empty fills again, you'll see.
quatrains.note: Draws on the classical pearl-and-oyster conceit familiar from Sufi didactic poetry: the drop of rain becomes a pearl only by consenting to confinement inside the shell. The Persian plays on the rhymes hur/durr/pur (free/pearl/full).

lines: افسوس که سرمایه ز کف بیرون شد
وز دست اجل بسی جگرها خون شد
کس نامَد از آن جهان که پُرسم از وی
کاحوال مسافران دنیا چون شد
quatrains.source_title: افسوس که سرمایه ز کف بیرون شد
literal: Alas, the capital has slipped through our fingers,
and at the hand of death many livers have turned to blood.
No one has come from that other world for me to ask
how matters stand for the travelers of this life.
poetic: Alas! our capital is spent and gone,
and death has wrung the hearts of countless ones.
No one returns from that far country's road
to tell me how those travelers fare beyond.
quatrains.note: The classic Khayyamian complaint against eschatological ignorance: no traveler ever comes back with a report. The word jegar (liver) was considered the seat of love and feeling in medieval Persian physiology.

lines: افسوس که نامهٔ جوانی طی شد
وان تازه بهار زندگانی دی شد
آن مرغ طرب که نام او بود شباب
فریاد ندانم که کی آمد کی شد
quatrains.source_title: افسوس که نامه جوانی طی شد
literal: Alas, the book of youth has been rolled up,
and that fresh springtime of life has become winter.
That bird of delight whose name was Youth—
I cry out, I don't know when it came or when it went.
poetic: Alas! the book of youth is closed and furled,
youth's fresh springtide has slipped into the cold.
That bird of joy whose name was Youth—
I cry, I never knew it come, or go.
quatrains.note: A tight image cluster: life as a rolled-up manuscript (namah), springtime turning to winter (di), and youth as a bird (morgh-e tarab) that flies off unseen. FitzGerald's 'Youth's sweet-scented manuscript' derives closely from this.

lines: ای بس که نباشیم و جهان خواهد بود
نی نام ز ما و نی نشان خواهد بود
زین پیش نبودیم و نبُد هیچ خلل
زین پس چو نباشیم همان خواهد بود
quatrains.source_title: ای بس که نباشیم و جهان خواهد بود
literal: So often we will not exist, and the world will still be here,
no name will remain of us, and no trace.
Before this we were not, and there was no flaw in things;
after this we shall not be, and it will be the same.
poetic: How often we'll be gone, the world still here—
no name of us, no trace, no memory.
Before, we were not, and nothing was the worse;
after, we will not be, and so it goes.
quatrains.note: Pure Epicurean consolation: symmetrical non-existence before birth and after death. The phrasing hich khalal (no flaw, no gap) echoes Lucretius' argument that pre-natal nothingness is no evil, so post-mortem nothingness should not be either.

lines: این عقل که در رَهِ سعادت پوید
روزی صدبار خود تُرا میگوید
دریاب تو این یکدم وقتت که نهٔ
آن تره که بدروند و دیگر روید
quatrains.source_title: این عقل که در ره سعادت پوید
literal: This intellect that chases after the road of happiness
tells you a hundred times a day:
'Seize this one breath of yours, for you are not
that green herb which, once cut, grows back again.'
poetic: This mind that hunts the road to happiness
tells you a hundred times a day, no less:
'Seize this one breath—you are not the grass
that sprouts back after mowing, more or less.'
quatrains.note: A carpe diem rooted in a natural image: humans, unlike herbs (tareh, greens), have no second growth. The verse uses aql (reason) to argue for hedonism, characteristic of Khayyam's rationalist streak against ascetic otherworldliness.

lines: این قافلهٔ عمر عجب میگذرد
دریاب دَمی که با طرب میگذرد
ساقی غم فردای حریفان چه خوری
پیش آر پیاله را که شب میگذرد
quatrains.source_title: این قافله عمر عجب میگذرد
literal: How strangely this caravan of life passes by.
Seize the moment that passes with joy.
Cupbearer, why grieve over the drinkers' tomorrow?
Bring the cup forward, for the night is passing.
poetic: Life's caravan is passing, marvelous, strange—
seize the joyful breath before it goes.
Saqi, why fret tomorrow's fate for friends?
Bring the cup—the night is slipping past.
quatrains.note: The caravan (qafilah) is a stock image for the procession of mortal life in Persian poetry. The address to the saqi (cupbearer) and the concrete urgency of night-passing both reappear in FitzGerald's 'Stars are setting, and the Caravan / Starts for the dawn of Nothing.'

lines: بر پشت من از زمانه تو می‌آید
وز من همه کار نانکو می‌آید
جان عزم رحیل کرد گفتم بِمرد
گفتا چکنم خانه فرو می‌آید
quatrains.source_title: بر پشت من از زمانه تو می‌آید
literal: From the wheel of time, pain comes upon my back.
And from me, every action comes out badly.
The soul decided to depart; I said, 'Stop!'
It said, 'What am I to do? The house is collapsing.'
poetic: Time lays its weight upon my aching back,
and every deed I turn to comes out wrong.
The soul prepared to leave. I cried, 'Stay on!'
'What can I do,' it said, 'the roof gives way.'
quatrains.note: The body imagined as a crumbling house the soul must quit: a stock Sufi and Aristotelian trope (the body as tenement of the rational soul). The quiet dialogue with one's own departing soul gives the quatrain a private, almost domestic feel.

lines: بر چرخ فلک هیچ کسی چیر نشد
وز خوردن آدمی زمین سیر نشد
مغرور بدانی که نخوردست تُرا
تعجیل نکن هم بخورد دیر نشد
quatrains.source_title: بر چرخ فلک هیچ کسی چیر نشد
literal: No one has ever prevailed over the turning sky,
and the earth has never grown full from eating human beings.
You are proud because it has not yet devoured you—
don't be in a hurry; it will eat you in time.
poetic: None has conquered the turning wheel of sky,
and earth is never sated, eating men.
You preen because it has not gulped you yet—
no rush: late or soon, it takes you then.
quatrains.note: The earth personified as an insatiable eater of mortals. The poem undercuts worldly pride with gallows-humor reassurance: your turn is only delayed. Compare Whinfield 137's Job-like complaint of a God who 'doth bruise full many a bosom day by day.'

lines: بر چشم تو عالم ارچه می‌آرایند
مَگرای بدان که عاقلان نَگرایند
بسیار چو تو روند و بسیار آیند
بربای نصیب خویش کت بربایند
quatrains.source_title: بر چشم تو عالم ارچه می‌آرایند
literal: Though the world is being dressed up before your eyes,
do not be drawn to it, for the wise are not drawn.
Many like you have gone and many will come;
snatch your share before it is snatched from you.
poetic: Though the world puts on finery before you,
do not be lured by it—the wise are not.
Many like you have gone, and many come;
seize your share before your share is caught.
quatrains.note: A cool warning against world-attachment (talab ud-dunya). The final line uses the same verb (bar-ba) twice in opposite senses—you snatch your portion before it snatches you—a compact example of Khayyam's fondness for play on a root.

lines: بر من قلم قضا چو بی من رانند
پس نیک و بَدَش ز من چرا میدانند
دی بی من و امروز چو دی بی من و تو
فردا بچه حجّتم بداور خوانند
quatrains.source_title: بر من قلم قضا چو بی من رانند
literal: When the pen of fate runs over me without me,
why, then, do they blame me for its good and bad?
Yesterday without me, today like yesterday without me and you,
tomorrow, with what argument can they summon me before the Judge?
poetic: Fate's pen runs over me without my say—
why blame me, then, for what its inkings do?
Yesterday without me, today the same;
tomorrow, how will they indict me, too?
quatrains.note: A direct challenge to predestinarian theology: if the decree is written without my consent, how can I be morally judged? The argument parallels Whinfield's No. 100 ('Without His will no act of mine was wrought; / Is it then just to punish me in hell?') almost point for point.

lines: تا چند اسیر رنگ و بو خواهی شد
چند از پی هر زشت و نکو خواهی شد
گر چشمهٔ زمزمیّ و گر آب حیات
آخر بدل خاک فرو خواهی شد
quatrains.source_title: تا چند اسیر رنگ و بو خواهی شد
literal: How long will you remain captive to color and scent?
How long will you chase after every ugly and fair thing?
Whether you are Zamzam's spring or the water of life,
in the end you will sink into dust.
poetic: How long, captive to color and to scent?
How long chase after each fair thing, each plain?
Though you be Zamzam's spring, or water of life,
at last you go down into dust again.
quatrains.note: Zamzam is the sacred well at Mecca; ab-e hayat is the legendary water of immortality sought by Khezr and Alexander. Even these storied waters end in dust—the leveling mortality Khayyam returns to often.

lines: تا راه قلندری نپوئی نشود
رخساره بخون دل نشوئی نشود
سودا چه پزی تا که چو دلسوختگان
آزاد بترک خود نگوئی نشود
quatrains.source_title: تا راه قلندری نپوئی نشود
literal: Until you take the qalandar's road, it will not happen.
Until you wash your face in heart's blood, it will not happen.
Why do you brew your schemes, when like the heart-burned ones
only by abandoning yourself can freedom come?
poetic: Till you walk the qalandar's road, no—
till you wash your face in heart's blood, no—
why brew your schemes? Like those the fire has burned,
only by losing self will freedom come.
quatrains.note: The qalandar is the antinomian Sufi wanderer; the 'heart-burned' (delsukhtegan) are those consumed in divine love. This quatrain is strikingly mystical for Khayyam and echoes the fana (self-annihilation) doctrine of the Sufi path.

lines: تا زهره و مه در آسمان گشت پدید
بهتر ز می ناب کسی هیچ ندید
من در عجبم ز میفروشان کایشان
به زانکه فروشند چه خواهند خرید
quatrains.source_title: تا زهره و مه در آسمان گشت پدید
literal: Since Venus and the moon appeared in the sky,
no one has seen anything better than clear wine.
I marvel at the wine-sellers: whatever they sell,
what could they possibly want to buy that is better?
poetic: Since Venus and the moon first lit the sky,
no one has seen a thing outshining wine.
I wonder at the vintners: what on earth
could they wish to purchase half as fine?
quatrains.note: The image of wine-sellers baffled by what they could possibly buy with their takings is one of Khayyam's most-loved conceits. FitzGerald expanded it into his famous 'I wonder often what the Vintners buy / One half so precious as the goods they sell.'

lines: چون روزی و عمر بیش و کم نتوان کرد
دل را بکَم و بیش دژم نتوان کرد
کار من و تو چنانکه رای من و تُست
از موم بدست خویش هم نتوان کرد
quatrains.source_title: چون روزی و عمر بیش و کم نتوان کرد
literal: Since neither the span nor the daily bread can be made more or less,
there is no use making the heart sad over more or less.
My work and yours is such that, despite your wisdom and mine,
not even from wax in our own hands can we shape it.
poetic: Since neither life nor bread will budge for us,
no point in souring the heart with more or less.
Our work, for all your wisdom, and for mine,
no hand can shape, not even out of wax.
quatrains.note: A fatalist argument paired with a craftsman's image: even the most pliant material (wax) will not submit to our will. The triple repetition of man-o-tu (me and you) builds a sense of shared human helplessness.

lines: حیّی که بقدرت سَرو رومی سازد
همواره همو کار عدو می‌سازد
گویند قرابه گر مسلمان نبود
او را تو چه گوئی که کدو می‌سازد
quatrains.source_title: حیی که بقدرت سرو رومی سازد
literal: The Living One who by his power shapes a Roman cypress
is the same one who makes the enemy's business.
They say, if a gourd-flask is not a Muslim,
what will you say of him who makes it into a gourd?
poetic: The Living One who shapes the stately cypress
is He who shapes the adversary, too.
They say the gourd-flask is no Muslim vessel—
then what of Him who makes it into one?
quatrains.note: A theological jab: if gourds used as wine-flasks are haram (forbidden), what of the Creator who grows them that shape? The pun turns on Hayy (the Living, a divine name) and qarabah (flask). The 'Roman cypress' (sarv-e rumi) is a poetic commonplace for the beloved's figure.

lines: در دهر چو آوازِ گُلِ تازه دهند
فرمای بُتا که می باندازه دهند
از حور و قصور وَز بهشت و دوزخ
فارغ بنشین که آن هر آوازه دهند
quatrains.source_title: در دهر چو آواز گل تازه دهند
literal: In this world, when they announce the arrival of fresh roses,
order, my idol, that they serve wine in measure.
As for houris and palaces and heaven and hell,
sit still and untroubled; all those are just rumors.
poetic: When word goes out, fresh roses are in bloom,
give order, love: let them pour measured wine.
As for the houris, palaces, heaven, hell—
sit easy; all those tales are just a rumor.
quatrains.note: Khayyam dismisses the full furniture of the afterlife—huri (paradisal maidens), qusur (palaces)—as avazeh (rumor, hearsay). The word bota (idol) is the standard term of endearment for the beloved and carries no iconoclastic sting.

lines: در دهر هر آنکه نیم نانی دارد
از بهر نشست آشیانی دارد
نه خادم کس بود نه مخدوم کسی
گو شاد بزی که خوش جهانی دارد
quatrains.source_title: در دهر هر آنکه نیم نانی دارد
literal: In this world, whoever has half a loaf of bread
and a nest in which to sit,
who is neither the servant of anyone nor lord over anyone—
tell him to live gladly: he has a good world.
poetic: Whoever in this world has half a loaf
and some small nest to shelter him from weather,
who serves no lord, whom no man serves in turn—
bid him live glad: his world is good enough.
quatrains.note: A straightforward encomium of the Epicurean-Stoic middle way: enough bread, a roof, and freedom from both servitude and lordship. The sentiment is close to Lucretius and to Horace's beatus ille.

lines: دهقانِ قضا بسی چو ما کِشت و درود
غم خوردن بیهوده نمیدارد سود
پُر کن قدح می بکفم در نه زود
تا باز خورم که بودنیها همه بود
quatrains.source_title: دهقان قضا بسی چو ما کشت و درود
literal: The farmer Fate has sown and reaped many like us.
Grieving uselessly brings no benefit.
Quickly fill the cup of wine and place it in my hand,
so I may drink again, since whatever had to be has been.
poetic: Fate's farmer has sown many crops like us,
and reaped them all. No profit comes from grief.
Fill the cup quickly—set it in my hand—
so I may drink again: the die is cast.
quatrains.note: Fate (qaza) as a farmer (dehqan) who sows and reaps human crops is an old Persian metaphor. The final phrase bu¯danihā hameh bud ('whatever was to be has been') is a Stoic shrug.

lines: روزی است خوش و هوا نه گرم است و نه سرد
ابر از رُخ گلزار همی شوید گرد
بلبل بزبان حالِ خود با گل زرد
فریاد همی کند که می باید خورد
quatrains.source_title: روزی است خوش و هوا نه گرم است و نه سرد
literal: It is a fine day, neither warm nor cold.
The cloud washes the dust from the rose garden's face.
The nightingale, in its own state-language, to the yellow rose,
cries out: 'Wine must be drunk!'
poetic: A lovely day—not warm, not cold—
cloud bathing the garden's rose-faced dust.
Nightingale cries to the yellow rose, in its own tongue,
'Drink! Drink! Wine must be drunk!'
quatrains.note: The Persian mise-en-scène of rose and nightingale (gol-o-bolbol) is so stock that a whole genre is named for it. Here the bulbul commands the rose itself to drink, a charming inversion of the usual lyric direction.

lines: زان پیش که بر سرت شبیخون آرند
فرمای که تا بادهٔ گلگون آرند
تو زر نهٔ ای غافل نادان که تُرا
در خاک نهند و باز بیرون آرند
quatrains.source_title: زان پیش که بر سرت شبیخون آرند
literal: Before they launch a night raid upon your head,
give order that they bring the rose-colored wine.
You are not gold, you heedless fool, that they would
put you in the earth and then dig you out again.
poetic: Before they fall upon your head in the night,
call for the rose-red wine—bring it, don't wait.
You are not gold, poor fool, that they should bury
your body once, and dig it up for gain.
quatrains.note: A witty put-down of human self-importance: no one will exhume you the way they dig up buried treasure. FitzGerald takes up the same figure in his stanza on the 'Golden Grain'—those buried are turned to no 'aureate earth.'

lines: عمرت تا کی بخود پرستی گذرد
یا در پی نیستی و هستی گذرد
می نوش که عمری که اجل در پی اوست
آن به که بخواب یا بمستی گذرد
quatrains.source_title: عمرت تا کی بخود پرستی گذرد
literal: How long will your life pass in self-worship,
or in chasing after not-being and being?
Drink wine, for a life whose heels are pursued by death—
it is better it pass in sleep or in drunkenness.
poetic: How long will life go by in self-regard,
or running after Being and Not-being?
Drink! for a life that has death on its heels
is best spent in sleep, or wine's oblivion.
quatrains.note: A direct dismissal of ontological speculation (hasti-o nisti, Being and Not-being—the technical terms of kalam theology) in favor of oblivion. Whinfield 183 translates the same argument almost verbatim.

lines: کس مشکل اسرار اجل را نگشاد
کس یک قدم از نهاد بیرون ننهاد
من مینگرم ز مُبتدی تا اُستاد
عجز است بدست هرکه از مادر زاد
quatrains.source_title: کس مشکل اسرار اجل را نگشاد
literal: No one has untied the knot of death's secret,
no one has taken a single step beyond the nature given.
I look from novice to master alike:
helplessness is in the hand of every one born of a mother.
poetic: No one has loosed the knot that death has tied,
no one has stepped one inch beyond his nature.
I look from the first novice to the last master—
helpless is every child of any mother.
quatrains.note: The central word 'ajz (impotence, helplessness) is the same term Sufi theology uses for the creaturely condition before God. Every human, novice or adept, is bound alike by mortality—a strong anti-intellectualist note.

lines: کم کُن طمع از جهان و میزی خورسند
وز نیک و بد زمانه بکسل پیوند
می در کف و زلف دلبری گیر که زود
هم بگذرد و نماند این روزی چند
quatrains.source_title: کم کن طمع از جهان و میزی خورسند
literal: Cut short your greed for the world and live contentedly,
and break connection with the good and bad of time.
Take the cup in hand and a beloved's lock, for soon
both will pass, and these few days will not remain.
poetic: Cut short your greed; live out your days content;
sever all ties with fortune's good or ill.
Cup in hand, the beloved's curl in the other—
soon both are gone. These few brief days don't fill.
quatrains.note: The sensual triad of cup (may), lock of hair (zolf-e delbari), and hastening time is one of the most compressed and often-quoted Khayyamian tableaux. Compare Whinfield 332, which develops the same three images.

lines: گرچه غم و رنج من درازی دارد
عیش و طرب تو سرفرازی دارد
بر هر دو مکن تکیه که دورانِ فلک
در پرده هزار گونه بازی دارد
quatrains.source_title: گرچه غم و رنج من درازی دارد
literal: Though my grief and suffering are long-drawn,
your pleasure and delight walk with a proud head.
Do not rely on either, for the turning of the sphere
has behind its curtain a thousand kinds of play.
poetic: Though my sorrow and pain stretch out at length,
your pleasure walks along with a lifted head—
trust neither; for behind the spinning heavens
a thousand kinds of strange play are bred.
quatrains.note: A measured warning against both despair and triumph. The image of dawran-e falak (turning of the sky) with a 'curtain' concealing its tricks is cognate with FitzGerald's 'inverted Bowl we call The Sky.'

lines: گردون ز زمین هیچ گلی بر نارد
کش نشکند و هم بزمین نسپارد
گر ابر چو آب خاک را بردارد
تا حشر همه خون عزیزان بارد
quatrains.source_title: گردون ز زمین هیچ گلی بر نارد
literal: The sky never raises a rose from the earth
without then breaking it and returning it to the earth.
If the cloud, like water, gathered up the dust,
until Judgment Day it would rain the blood of the beloved.
poetic: The sky raises no rose from the earth
that it does not crush and return to dust.
If clouds could gather earth the way they gather water,
till Judgment Day they'd rain our loved ones' blood.
quatrains.note: A darker variant of FitzGerald's 'never blows so red / The Rose as where some buried Caesar bled': here the claim is that all roses are beloved-dust, and if the sky could distill earth it would rain only blood. One of Khayyam's most compressed and macabre images.

lines: گر یک نَفست ز زندگانی گذرد
مگذار که جز بشادمانی گذرد
هُشدار که سرمایهٔ سودای جهان
عمر است چنان کش گذرانی گذرد
quatrains.source_title: گر یک نفست ز زندگانی گذرد
literal: If a single breath of yours goes by out of this life,
do not let it pass except in gladness.
Be warned: the capital of this world's commerce
is life itself—it passes just as you let it pass.
poetic: If one more breath goes by out of your life,
do not let it pass except in joy.
Be warned: the stock-in-trade of this whole traffic
is life—and it passes just as you employ.
quatrains.note: Uses the mercantile metaphor of sarmayeh (capital) that recurs in several Khayyam quatrains: life is the one currency we spend. A Stoic-Epicurean injunction to mindful enjoyment, without otherworldly deferral.

lines: گویند بهشت و حور عین خواهد بود
آنجا می و شیر و انگبین خواهد بود
گر ما می و معشوق گزیدیم چه باک
چون عاقبتِ کار چنین خواهد بود
quatrains.source_title: گویند بهشت و حور عین خواهد بود
literal: They say there will be paradise and bright-eyed houris,
and there will be wine and milk and honey.
If we have chosen wine and a beloved—what's the harm,
since in the end that is how it all ends up?
poetic: They say there will be houris and a heaven,
and wine and milk and honey pouring free.
If we have chosen wine and beloved here,
what's the harm, since that is all eternity?
quatrains.note: A cheeky argument from consistency: if paradise is wine and lovers, we are already there. Whinfield 185 ('If these be lawful in the world to come, / Surely 'tis right to love them here as well') captures the same logic.

lines: گویند بهشت و حور و کوثر باشد
جویِ می و شیر و شهد و شکّر باشد
پُر کُن قدح باده و بر دستم نه
نقدی ز هزار نسیه خوشتر باشد
quatrains.source_title: گویند بهشت و حور و کوثر باشد
literal: They say there will be paradise and houris and Kauthar,
streams of wine and milk and honey and sugar.
Fill the cup of wine and place it in my hand—
ready cash is better than a thousand promises.
poetic: They say there'll be paradise and streams of wine,
Kauthar, with milk and honey, sugar, too.
Fill the wine-cup, and set it in my hand—
ready cash beats a thousand IOUs.
quatrains.note: Kauthar is the paradisal river promised in Qur'an 108. The 'cash vs. credit' antithesis (naqd vs. nasi'a) is one of Khayyam's signature tropes and the clear source for FitzGerald's 'take the Cash and let the Credit go.'

lines: گویند هر آنکسان که با پرهیزند
زانسان که بمیرند چنان برخیزند
ما با می و معشوقه از آنیم مُدام
باشد که بحشرمان چنان انگیزند
quatrains.source_title: گویند هر آنکسان که با پرهیزند
literal: They say: those who are the abstemious ones
will be raised up in the same state they died in.
We are forever with wine and a beloved—for that reason
perhaps on Resurrection Day they will raise us the same.
poetic: They say: the ones who lived abstemious here
will rise in the same shape in which they died.
We, then, are always with our wine and love,
so we'll be raised that way, on Judgment's tide.
quatrains.note: A syllogism played for comic effect, building on the hadith-inspired belief that one is resurrected in the posture and state of death. 'Die drunk with the beloved, rise drunk with the beloved'—a sly turning of orthodoxy against itself.

lines: می خور که ز دل کثرت و قلّت ببرد
و اندیشهٔ هفتاد و دو ملّت ببرد
پرهیز مکن ز کیمیائی که از او
یک جرعه خوری هزار علّت ببرد
quatrains.source_title: می خور که ز دل کثرت و قلت ببرد
literal: Drink wine, for it removes abundance and want from the heart,
and carries off the anxiety of the seventy-two sects.
Do not shun that alchemy of which, if you take
a single sip, it removes a thousand ailments.
poetic: Drink! it strips the heart of too-much and too-little,
and carries off the seventy-two creeds' care.
Do not forsake that alchemy: one sip,
and a thousand ailments vanish in the air.
quatrains.note: The 'seventy-two sects' is a standard Muslim reckoning (based on a hadith about the umma's divisions), here neatly dismissed by a draft of wine. FitzGerald's 'Grape that can with Logic absolute / The Two-and-Seventy jarring Sects confute' is a near-direct translation.

lines: هر راز که اندر دل دانا باشد
باید که نهفته‌تر ز عنقا باشد
کاندر صدف از نهفتگی گردد دُر
آن قطره که رازِ دلِ دریا باشد
quatrains.source_title: هر راز که اندر دل دانا باشد
literal: Every secret that lies in the heart of the wise
must be more hidden than the Simurgh.
For within the shell, by hiddenness it becomes a pearl—
that drop which is the secret of the sea's heart.
poetic: Every secret held in a wise heart
must be more hidden than the Simurgh's nest.
Within the shell, by hiddenness, a drop
becomes the pearl—the sea's own secret, pressed.
quatrains.note: The 'Anqa/Simurgh is the legendary, never-seen bird of Persian mythology, here the metaphor of perfect concealment. The pearl-in-shell image recurs from #61; hiddenness is the condition of preciousness. Echoes a Sufi adab of discretion.

lines: هر صبح که روی لاله شبنم گیرد
بالای بنفشه در چمن خم گیرد
انصاف مرا ز غنچه خوش میآید
کو دامنِ خویشتن فراهم گیرد
quatrains.source_title: هر صبح که روی لاله شبنم گیرد
literal: Each morning, when the tulip's cheek catches the dew
and the violet in the meadow bends its head low,
honestly, I take delight in the rose-bud—
how it gathers its own skirts together.
poetic: Each dawn when the tulip's cheek takes on dew
and the violet bows its head low in the field,
in truth, the rosebud is the one I love—
how it keeps its own skirts gathered and concealed.
quatrains.note: A quiet nature-miniature. The ghoncheh (rosebud) gathering its skirts is, in Persian convention, an emblem of modesty and self-possession, contrasted with the dew-struck tulip and bowed violet. One of Khayyam's gentler observations.

lines: هرگز دل من ز علم محروم نشد
کم ماند ز اسرار که معلوم نشد
هفتاد و دو سال فکر کردم شب و روز
معلومم شد که هیچ معلوم نشد
quatrains.source_title: هرگز دل من ز علم محروم نشد
literal: My heart was never deprived of learning;
few were the secrets that were not made known to me.
For seventy-two years, night and day, I thought and thought—
what became known to me is that nothing became known.
poetic: My heart has never been starved of learning;
few were the secrets left beyond my sight.
Seventy-two years, I thought by day and night—
and what I learned was: nothing is learned right.
quatrains.note: A direct confession of the failure of rationalist inquiry, culminating in the famous line hich ma'lumam nashod ('nothing became known to me'). Seventy-two is chosen for its resonance with the seventy-two sects (cf. #90). The tradition ascribes this to Khayyam's own last word on learning.

lines: هم دانهٔ امید بخرمن ماند
هم باغ و سرای بی تو و من ماند
سیم و زر خویش از دِرَمی تا بجوی
با دوست بخور گرنه بدشمن ماند
quatrains.source_title: هم دانه امید بخرمن ماند
literal: The seed of hope will remain in the granary,
and the garden and house will remain without you and me.
Your silver and gold, from a dirham to a jow's-worth—
eat it with a friend, or it will fall to the enemy.
poetic: The seed of hope stays in the granary still,
the garden and the house go on without us.
Your silver and your gold, from coin to grain—
share them with a friend, or the enemy will feast.
quatrains.note: A practical motto: enjoy your wealth with those you love, because you cannot take it and strangers will inherit. Compare the Qohelet-like sentiment in Whinfield 202 ('feast with friends, ere this warm breath of thine / Be chilled in death').

lines: یارانِ موافق همه از دست شدند
در پای اجل یکان یکان پست شدند
خوردیم ز یک شراب در مجلس عمر
دوری دو سه پیشتر ز ما مست شدند
quatrains.source_title: یاران موافق همه از دست شدند
literal: The congenial companions have all slipped away,
one by one laid low at the foot of death.
We drank of the same wine in life's gathering—
a round or two before us, they became drunk and gone.
poetic: Our good companions have all slipped away,
one by one brought low at the feet of death.
We drank of the same wine at life's table;
a round or two ahead, they lost their breath.
quatrains.note: The 'round or two before' (dawri do seh pishtar) is precisely the image FitzGerald made famous in 'drunk their Cup a Round or two before, / And one by one crept silently to Rest.' A direct source quatrain.

lines: یک جام شراب صد دل و دین ارزد
یک جرعهٔ می مملکت چین ارزد
جز بادهٔ لعل نیست در روی زمین
تخمی که هزار جان شیرین ارزد
quatrains.source_title: یک جام شراب صد دل و دین ارزد
literal: One cup of wine is worth a hundred hearts and religions.
One sip of wine is worth the kingdom of China.
There is nothing on the face of the earth but ruby wine—
a seed that is worth a thousand sweet lives.
poetic: One cup of wine outweighs a hundred faiths,
a sip of it outweighs the realm of China.
There is nothing on the face of earth like wine—
one grain worth a thousand sweet lives in it.
quatrains.note: A maximal valuation of wine as the sole unequivocal good. Mamlakat-e Chin (the kingdom of China) was proverbial for boundless wealth. Whinfield 64 uses the near-identical 'realm of Tus, Throne of Kobad and crown of Kai Kawus.'

lines: یک قطرهٔ آب بود با دریا شد
یک ذرّهٔ خاک با زمین یکتا شد
آمد شدنِ تو اندرین عالم چیست
آمد مگسی پدید و ناپیدا شد
quatrains.source_title: یک قطره آب بود با دریا شد
literal: A drop of water was, and it became the sea;
a speck of earth was, and became one with the land.
What is your coming and going in this world?
A fly appeared, and then was not seen.
poetic: A drop of water fell, and was the sea;
a grain of dust, and was the earth below.
What is your coming, going, in this world?
A fly that for a moment showed, then no.
quatrains.note: Two cosmic mergings—drop into sea, dust into earth—followed by the deflating image of a passing fly. The fly (magas) is a deliberately humble vehicle, undercutting any grand metaphysics of selfhood. Compare the Sufi doctrine of reabsorption in the divine.

lines: یک نان بدو روز اگر بود حاصلِ مرد
وز کوزه شکستهٔ دَمی آبی سرد
مأمور کم از خودی چرا باید بود
یا خدمت چون خودی چرا باید کرد
quatrains.source_title: یک نان بدو روز اگر بود حاصل مرد
literal: If a man has one loaf of bread to last two days,
and a moment's cold water from a broken jug,
why should he be the subordinate of one lesser than himself?
Or why should he have to serve one of his own kind?
poetic: If you have bread for two days' meals in store,
a sip of cold from a cracked jug beside you,
why be the lackey of some lesser man?
Why serve your equal, and suffer him to guide you?
quatrains.note: A robust anti-servility poem: a broken jug and stale bread are preferable to patronage. The phrasing khodmat-e chun khodi ('service of one like yourself') rejects even peer-dependence. Whinfield 207 renders this nearly word-for-word.

lines: آن لعل در آبگینهٔ ساده بیار
وان محرم و مونس هر آزاده بیار
چون میدانی که مدّت عالم خاک
باد است که زود بگذرد باده بیار
quatrains.source_title: آن لعل در آبگینه ساده بیار
literal: Bring that ruby in plain crystal,
and that intimate and companion of every free soul.
