Since you know that the span of the world of dust
is wind that quickly passes—bring wine!
poetic: Bring out that ruby in its crystal glass,
the confidant and friend of every free one.
Since you know this world of dust's long span
is wind that passes quickly—bring the wine on!
quatrains.note: Azadeh ('free one,' 'noble one') is a favorite Khayyam term for the drinker who has liberated himself from theological anxiety. The ruby-in-crystal is wine in a clear glass. The closing imperative badeh biyar ('bring wine!') is the quatrain's emphatic refrain.

lines: از بودنی ایدوست چه داری تیمار
وز فکرت بیهوده دل و جان افکار
خرّم بزی و جهان بشادی گذران
تدبیر نه با تو کرده‌اند اوّل کار
quatrains.source_title: از بودنی ایدوست چه داری تیمار
literal: O friend, what care do you have for what must be?
Why wound your heart and soul with useless thought?
Live joyfully, pass through the world in gladness—
you were not consulted when the plan was first made.
poetic: Friend, why trouble with what must be?
Why wound your heart with futile thinking?
Live in joy, go through the world in gladness—
no one consulted you at the first drinking.
quatrains.note: The rhetorical climax—'the plan was made without consulting you'—turns Ash'arite predestinarian theology into a license for cheerfulness rather than anxiety. Whinfield 241 ('He formed them all without consulting thee') is the direct rendering.

lines: افلاک که جز غم نفزایند دگر
ننهند بجا تا نربایند دگر
نا آمدگان اگر بدانند که ما
از دهر چه میکشیم نایند دگر
quatrains.source_title: افلاک که جز غم نفزایند دگر
literal: The heavens, which bring forth only sorrow anew,
will not leave a thing in place, only to snatch it anew.
If the not-yet-come knew what we endure
from this age, they would not come at all.
poetic: The heavens that bring only fresh sorrow
set nothing up except to tear it down.
Those yet to come, if they but knew what we
endure here, would not come at all, I'll vow.
quatrains.note: A classic pessimist trope: the never-to-be-born would refuse the journey. Compare the chorus of Sophocles's Oedipus at Colonus ('never to have been born surpasses all reckoning') and Whinfield 240 ('would they rather come or stay?').

lines: ای دل غم این جهان فرسوده مخور
بیهوده نهٔ غمان بیهوده مخور
چون بوده گذشت و نیست نابوده پدید
خوش باش غم بوده و نابوده مخور
quatrains.source_title: ای دل غم این جهان فرسوده مخور
literal: O heart, do not eat the sorrow of this worn-out world.
You are not useless—so do not eat useless sorrows.
Since what was has gone, and what was not is not yet visible,
be glad: do not eat the grief of what was or was not.
poetic: O heart, stop eating this worn-out world's sorrow;
useless griefs are not worth useless eating.
The past has gone, the future is not yet;
be glad—no grief can alter either greeting.
quatrains.note: The threefold repetition of bihudah (useless, vain) turns the quatrain into a near-mantra against self-inflicted anguish. The logic—past is gone, future is not yet—is stock Stoicism and recurs in Whinfield 278.

lines: ایدل همه اسباب جهان خواسته گیر
باغ طربت بسبزه آراسته گیر
وانگاه بر آن سبزه شبی چون شبنم
بنشسته و بامداد برخاسته گیر
quatrains.source_title: ایدل همه اسباب جهان خواسته گیر
literal: O heart, take all the goods of the world as already gained,
your garden of delight as already decked with green,
and then think of yourself, on that green, one night like dew,
sitting down, and by morning—already risen and gone.
poetic: O heart, count the world's goods as all gained,
your garden of pleasure already decked in green;
now think: on that green, one night, dew-wise you sit,
and by morning have risen, and are unseen.
quatrains.note: A thought experiment that leans into its own image: grant yourself every good, then see how brief the sitting is. The dew-on-grass conceit for human life is paralleled in Whinfield 243 and has biblical echoes (Psalm 103).

lines: این اهل قبور خاک گشتند و غبار
هر ذرّه ز هر ذرّه گرفتند کنار
آه این چه شراب است که تا روز شمار
بیخود شده و بیخبرند از همه کار
quatrains.source_title: این اهل قبور خاک گشتند و غبار
literal: These people of the graves have become dust and powder,
each speck has taken its place apart from every other speck.
Ah, what wine is this that, till Judgment Day,
they are out of themselves and unaware of all affairs?
poetic: These people of the graves have turned to dust,
each mote apart from every other mote.
What wine is this that, till the Reckoning's Day,
they lie unconscious, senseless, past report?
quatrains.note: An ironic inversion: the sober dead are imagined as the most thoroughly drunk—'out of themselves' (bekhod) until Judgment. The word khakbar ('dust-bearing') foregrounds the physical dissolution behind the metaphor.

lines: خشت سر خم ز ملکت جم خوشتر
بوی قدح از غذای مریم خوشتر
آه سحری ز سینهٔ خمّاری
از نالهٔ بوسعید و ادهم خوشتر
quatrains.source_title: خشت سر خم ز ملکت جم خوشتر
literal: The brick at the mouth of the wine-jar is finer than Jamshid's kingdom;
the scent of the cup is finer than Miriam's fare.
The dawn sigh from the chest of a wine-seller
is finer than the lament of Bu Sa'id and Adham.
poetic: The brick stopping the wine-jar outshines Jamshid's kingdom;
the cup's scent, the fare Mary fed her son.
A wine-seller's dawn sigh, breathed out in the tavern,
is worth the lament of Adham and Bu Sa'id, rolled in one.
quatrains.note: A deliberate provocation ranking the tavern above the sacred: Jamshid's jeweled cup (the seven-ringed seeing-bowl of Persian legend), Miriam's miraculous food (Qur'an 19), and the moans of the famous ascetics Bu Sa'id b. Abu'l-Khayr and Ibrahim b. Adham are all outdone by a wine-jar's brick. Whinfield 253 renders the same ranking.

lines: در دایرهٔ سپهر ناپیدا غور
جامی است که جمله را چشانند بدور
نوبت چو بدور تو رسد آه مکن
می نوش بخوشدلی که دور است نه جور
quatrains.source_title: در دایره سپهر ناپیدا غور
literal: In the circle of the sphere whose depth is unseen,
there is a cup that is given to all in turn.
When the turn reaches you, do not groan:
drink wine with good cheer, for it is a turn, not tyranny.
poetic: In the sphere's vast turn, whose depth is unseen,
there is one cup that goes around to all.
When its turn reaches you, do not groan—
drink it with cheer: a turn, not a brawl.
quatrains.note: The wordplay turns on dawr, meaning both 'turn' (a round of drinks) and 'cycle' (of fate), matched with jawr (tyranny) at line's end. Everyone gets the same cup in turn; the heavens are fair in that one sense. Whinfield 254 translates closely.

lines: دی کوزه گری بدیدم اندر بازار
بر پاره گِلی لگد همی زد بسیار
و آن گِل بزبان حال با او میگفت
من همچو تو بوده‌ام مرا نیکو دار
quatrains.source_title: دی کوزه گری بدیدم اندر بازار
literal: Yesterday I saw a potter in the market,
kicking and kicking a lump of clay.
And that clay, in the state-language, said to him:
'I was once like you—treat me well.'
poetic: Yesterday, in the market, I saw a potter
kicking and kicking a lump of clay.
And the clay, in its own silent tongue, said:
'I was once like you—treat me well today.'
quatrains.note: One of the most famous of all Khayyam quatrains—the direct source for FitzGerald's 'I watch'd the Potter thumping his wet Clay ... Gently, Brother, gently, pray!' Whinfield 252 translates it nearly verbatim.

lines: زان می که حیات جاودانی است بخور
سرمایهٔ لذّت جوانی است بخور
سوزنده چو آتش است لیکن غم را
سازنده چو آب زندگانی است بخور
quatrains.source_title: زان می که حیات جاودانی است بخور
literal: Of that wine which is eternal life, drink!
The capital of the pleasure of youth—drink!
Like fire, it is a burner; but for grief,
it is a mender like the water of life—drink!
poetic: Drink of that wine that is eternal life.
Drink—it is the capital of youth's pleasure.
It burns like fire; but against grief
it repairs like the water of life, past measure.
quatrains.note: Uses two classical topoi: hayat-e javedani (eternal life) and ab-e zindagani (Khezr's legendary water of immortality). The paradox that fire and healing water are the same drink compresses the whole Epicurean defense of wine.

lines: گر باده خوری تو با خردمندان خور
یا با صنمی لاله رخی خندان خور
بسیار مخور وِرْدْ مکُن فاش مساز
اندک خور و گَه گاه خور و پنهان خور
quatrains.source_title: گر باده خوری تو با خردمندان خور
literal: If you drink wine, drink it with the wise,
or with a tulip-cheeked, laughing idol.
Do not drink much; do not make a public litany of it, do not broadcast it.
Drink little, drink now and then, drink in hiding.
poetic: If you drink wine, drink it among the wise,
or with a tulip-cheeked, laughing beloved.
Do not drink much. Do not chant of it in public.
Drink little. Drink sometimes. Drink unobserved.
quatrains.note: A prudential code: the wise company, the secret measure, the small cup. Khayyam here sounds almost like a Confucian ritualist, guarding pleasure from both excess and scandal. Compare Whinfield 195 on the 'casuistry of wine.'

lines: وقت سحر است خیز ای طرفه پسر
پُر باده لعل کُن بلورین ساغر
کاین یکدم عاریت در این کُنج فنا
بسیار بجوئیّ و نیابی دیگر
quatrains.source_title: وقت سحر است خیز ای طرفه پسر
literal: It is the time of dawn—arise, O marvelous boy!
Fill the crystal cup full of ruby wine.
For this one borrowed breath in the corner of non-being
you will search for long and never find again.
poetic: It is the dawn—arise, O marvelous boy!
Fill the crystal goblet with ruby wine.
This single borrowed breath in the niche of Nothing—
look long, and never find its like again.
quatrains.note: The 'borrowed breath' ('ariyat) is a recurring Khayyam term: life as loan. Kunj-e fana ('corner of annihilation') is vintage Sufi vocabulary pressed into Epicurean service—the cosmos as a tiny nook in the void.

lines: از جملهٔ رفتگان این راه دراز
باز آمده کیست تا بما گوید راز
پس بر سر این دو راههٔ آز و نیاز
تا هیچ نمانی که نمی‌آئی باز
quatrains.source_title: از جمله رفتگان این راه دراز
literal: Of all those who have gone down this long road,
who has come back to tell us the secret?
So, at this crossroads of greed and need,
leave nothing undone—for you will not come again.
poetic: Of all who have gone down this long, long road,
who has returned to tell us what he saw?
At this forked path between our greed and need,
leave nothing undone—there is no coming back.
quatrains.note: The core agnostic complaint: no eyewitness of the afterlife has ever returned. FitzGerald's 'Strange, is it not? that of the myriads who / Before us pass'd the door of Darkness through, / Not one returns' is a direct versification. Whinfield 129 and 258 both render it.

lines: ای پیر خردمند پگه‌تر برخیز
وان کودک خاک بیز را بنگر تیز
پندش ده و گو که نرم نرمک می‌بیز
مغزِ سَرِ کیقباد و چشم پرویز
quatrains.source_title: ای پیر خردمند پگه‌تر برخیز
literal: O wise old man, rise earlier,
and look sharply at that child sifting dust.
Give him advice and say: 'Sift gently, little by little—
the brain of Kaikobad's skull, the eye of Parviz.'
poetic: Old wise one, rise earlier than you used;
sharpen your gaze at that child sifting dust.
Instruct him: 'Sift lightly, bit by bit—
here is Kaikobad's brain; here Parviz's eye to trust.'
quatrains.note: Kaikobad and Khosrau Parviz are legendary Iranian kings (Shahnameh and Sasanian history). The poem imagines their very skulls now in a child's dust-sifter. The FitzGerald tradition of Caesar's clay blowing in the wind draws on this cluster of Khayyamian images.

lines: وقت سحر است خیز ای مایهٔ ناز
نرمک نرمک باده خور و چنگ نواز
کانها که بجایند نپایند بسی
وانها که شدند کس نمی‌آید باز
quatrains.source_title: وقت سحر است خیز ای مایه ناز
literal: It is the time of dawn—arise, O object of tenderness!
Drink wine gently, gently, and strike the harp.
For those who are still here will not last long,
and those who are gone—no one returns.
poetic: It is the dawn—arise, O tender one!
Drink the wine softly. Strike the harp again.
Those still among us will not linger long,
and those who have gone, no one sees again.
quatrains.note: A gentler, almost lullaby variant of quatrain 111: no one returns, so drink softly, touch the harp. The adverb narmak narmak (very gently) lends the quatrain its hushed mood. Compare Whinfield 129.

lines: مرغی دیدم نشسته بر بارهٔ طوس
در پیش نهاده کلّه کیکاوس
با کلّه همی گفت که افسوس افسوس
کو بانگ جرسها و کجا نالهٔ کوس
quatrains.source_title: مرغی دیدم نشسته بر باره طوس
literal: I saw a bird perched on the wall of Tus,
the skull of Kai-Kavus laid before it.
It was saying to the skull: 'Alas, alas—
where is the sound of bells? where the boom of war-drums?'
poetic: I saw a bird perched on the wall of Tus,
Kai-Kavus's skull laid out before its gaze.
It was saying to the skull: 'Alas, alas—
where the camel-bells? the kettledrums of days?'
quatrains.note: Kai-Kavus is the Kayanid king of the Shahnameh whose flying throne once rivaled the sky; Tus was the ancient capital near Nishapur. Whinfield 277 is a verbatim rendering. FitzGerald's Persepolis-ringdove quatrain (from his notes to stanza 18) draws on the same imagination.

lines: جامی است که عقل آفرین میزندش
صد بوسه ز مهر بر جبین میزندش
این کوزه‌گر دهر چنین جام لطیف
میسازد و باز بر زمین میزندش
quatrains.source_title: جامی است که عقل آفرین میزندش
literal: It is a cup for which reason calls out praise
and plants a hundred kisses of love upon its brow.
Yet this potter of the age makes such a delicate cup
and then dashes it again upon the ground.
poetic: A cup that reason crowns with praise,
on whose brow love plants a hundred kisses—
and yet the potter of this age makes such a fine one
and dashes it again against the earth, unmisses.
quatrains.note: The human body as a delicately wrought cup, lovingly made and casually shattered. A Job-like protest: 'Thine hands have fashioned me; yet Thou dost destroy me.' Whinfield 290 makes the complaint explicit.

lines: خیّام اگر ز باده مستی خوش باش
با ماه رخی اگر نشستی خوش باش
چون عاقبتِ کارِ جهان نیستی است
انگار که نیستی چو هستی خوش باش
quatrains.source_title: خیام اگر ز باده مستی خوش باش
literal: Khayyam, if you are drunk with wine, be happy.
If you sit with a moon-faced one, be happy.
Since the end of the world's work is nothingness,
imagine you are non-existent—since you exist, be happy.
poetic: Khayyam, if you are drunk with wine, be glad.
If you sit with a moon-faced one, be glad.
Since the end of the world's whole work is nothing,
imagine you're not—and since you are, be glad.
quatrains.note: A perfectly balanced carpe-diem rondo: the poem names itself ('Khayyam') and offers a formal instruction to joy. The final move—'imagine you don't exist, and since you do, rejoice'—is pure Khayyamian consolation-through-nihil.

lines: در کارگه کوزه گری رفتم دوش
دیدم دو هزار کوزه گویا و خموش
ناگاه یکی کوزه برآورد خروش
کو کوزه گر و کوزه خر و کوزه فروش
quatrains.source_title: در کارگه کوزه گری رفتم دوش
literal: Last night I went to the potter's workshop,
and saw two thousand pots, some speaking, some silent.
Suddenly one pot raised a cry:
'Where is the potter, the pot-buyer, and the pot-seller?'
poetic: Last night I went into the potter's shop
and saw two thousand pots, some mute, some loud.
Suddenly one pot raised up a cry:
'Where is the potter? Where, the buyer and seller of the crowd?'
quatrains.note: The source quatrain for FitzGerald's entire Kuza-Nama cycle: a voice from among the shaped clay demands 'Who is the Potter, pray, and who the Pot?' Whinfield 283 gives a close prose-verse rendering. The scene also appears in Attar's Conference of the Birds as a topos.

lines: ایّام زمانه از کسی دارد ننگ
کو در غم ایّام نشیند دلتنگ
می خور تو در آبگینه با نالهٔ چنگ
زان پیش که آبگینه آید بر سنگ
quatrains.source_title: ایام زمانه از کسی دارد ننگ
literal: The days of fortune feel shame before anyone
who sits in the grief of time, heart-sunken.
Drink wine in a crystal cup, with the harp's lament,
before the crystal falls upon the stone.
poetic: The days of time are shamed before the man
who sits heart-sunken in their sorrow, pale.
Drink from the crystal cup, to the harp's lament,
before the cup falls on the stone, and fails.
quatrains.note: The ingenious final image: the drinker's glass and the drinker's life are both abgineh (crystal)—both will shatter. The first couplet's moral inversion—time is ashamed of the griever—is an unusual Khayyamian flourish.

lines: از جرم گِلِ سیاه تا اوج زُحل
کردم همه مشکلات کلّی را حل
بگشادم بندهای مشکل بحیل
هر بند گشاده شد بجز بند اجل
quatrains.source_title: از جرم گل سیاه تا اوج زحل
literal: From the body of black clay up to the height of Saturn,
I solved all the universal problems.
I undid the knots of every difficulty by cleverness.
Every knot came undone, except the knot of death.
poetic: From black earth's clay up to the height of Saturn,
I solved all the great puzzles one by one.
Every hard knot I loosened by my wit—
every one, except the knot of death, undone.
quatrains.note: A precise source for FitzGerald's 'Up from Earth's Center through the seventh Gate / I rose, and on the Throne of Saturn sate, / And many a Knot unravel'd by the Road; / But not the Master-knot of Human Fate.' Whinfield 303 translates the same quatrain.

lines: با سروقدی تازه‌تر از خرمن گل
از دست منه جام می و دامن گُل
زان پیش که ناگه شود از باد اجل
پیراهن عمر ما چو پیراهن گُل
quatrains.source_title: با سروقدی تازه‌تر از خرمن گل
literal: With one cypress-statured, fresher than a heap of roses,
do not let go of the wine-cup and the rose's skirt.
Before the wind of death should suddenly make
the garment of our life like the garment of a rose.
poetic: With one cypress-slim, fresher than a heap of roses,
do not release the cup, nor the rose's skirt—
before the sudden wind of death shall make
the garment of our life like the rose's, torn apart.
quatrains.note: The scattering rose-petal as a figure for the body dissolving in death is one of Persian poetry's most persistent images. The 'cypress-statured' beloved, the wine-cup, and the rose compose the standard triad of delight; the 'wind of death' (bad-e ajal) scatters them all.

lines: ای دوست بیا تا غم فردا نخوریم
وین یکدم عمر را غنیمت شمریم
فردا که ازین دیر فنا درگذریم
با هفت هزار سالگان سربسریم
quatrains.source_title: ای دوست بیا تا غم فردا نخوریم
literal: O friend, come, let us not eat tomorrow's grief,
and let us count this one breath of life as a windfall.
Tomorrow, when we pass through this transient inn,
we will be shoulder to shoulder with those seven thousand years old.
poetic: Friend, let tomorrow's sorrow keep its own account;
this one stolen breath is plunder enough for us.
Tomorrow, crossing through the vanishing caravansary,
we'll march beside the dead of seven thousand years.
quatrains.note: The "seven thousand years" is a traditional Persian reckoning of the age of the world; Khayyam's point is that our fleeting moment joins an already enormous crowd of the gone. FitzGerald famously fuses the image with "fill the Cup that clears Today" in his XXI/21.

lines: این چرخِ فلک که ما در او حیرانیم
فانوس خیال ازو مثالی دانیم
خورشید چراغدان و عالم فانوس
ما چون صُوَریم کاندر او حیرانیم
quatrains.source_title: این چرخ فلک که ما در او حیرانیم
literal: This wheel of heaven, at which we stand bewildered,
we see as a likeness of the phantom-lantern:
the sun is the lamp-holder, the world the lantern,
and we are like the figures inside, spinning in wonder.
poetic: This wheel of sky that keeps us dazed and reeling
is nothing but a phantom-lantern turning:
the sun its lamp, the world its painted drum,
and we the shadow-shapes that flicker round.
quatrains.note: The fanus-e khiyal is the revolving magic lantern of Persian bazaars — painted cylinders that spun around a candle. This is FitzGerald's direct source for "a moving row of Magic Shadow-shapes" in stanza LXVIII/68.

lines: برخیز ز خواب تا شرابی بخوریم
زان پیش که از زمانه تابی بخوریم
کاین چرخ ستیزه‌روی ناگه روزی
چندان ندهد زمان که آبی بخوریم
quatrains.source_title: برخیز ز خواب تا شرابی بخوریم
literal: Get up from sleep so we may drink a little wine,
before time wrings us with its twisting grip;
because this quarrelsome wheel will suddenly, one day,
give us no time even to swallow a sip of water.
poetic: Up from your sleep — let's drink, and drink at once,
before the wheel's rough hand has twisted us;
this brawling sky on some ungentle day
won't give us time to gulp a mouthful down.
quatrains.note: Persian tab khordan ("to take a twist / a scolding") puns on the body being wrung like wet cloth. The sudden snapping of life is a recurring Khayyam image, and a cousin of FG's "Bird of Time has but a little way to fly."

lines: برخیزم و عزم بادهٔ ناب کنم
رنگ رُخِ خود برنگ عنّاب کنم
این عقل فضول پیشه را مشتی می
بر روی زنم چنانکه در خواب کنم
quatrains.source_title: برخیزم و عزم باده ناب کنم
literal: I will rise up and set my mind on pure wine,
I will color my cheek the crimson of jujube;
this nosy intellect, forever meddling — a fist of wine
I'll throw in its face, to put it to sleep.
poetic: Up, then — and fix my heart on unmixed wine;
I'll stain these cheeks the red of jujube fruit.
This fussy, meddling intellect of mine —
a fist of wine across the face should put it out.
quatrains.note: Compare FG's "Divorced old barren Reason from my Bed" (FG 1st XL/5th LV): Khayyam's rougher version is to knock reason unconscious rather than divorce it. The annab (jujube) is a small crimson date-fruit, a classic Persian simile for flushed cheeks.

lines: بر مفرش خاک خفتگان می‌بینم
در زیرِ زمین نهفتگان می‌بینم
چندانکه بصحرای عدم مینگرم
ناآمدگان و رفتگان می‌بینم
quatrains.source_title: بر مفرش خاک خفتگان می‌بینم
literal: On the carpet of dust I see the sleepers;
beneath the earth I see those hidden away;
as far as I look into the plain of non-being,
I see the not-yet-come and the already-gone.
poetic: I see them stretched asleep on earth's long mat,
and those already folded underground;
and everywhere I turn — out on the waste of absence —
the not-yet-arrived, the long-departed crowds.
quatrains.note: Sahra-ye adam ("desert of non-being") is a standard Sufi-Neoplatonic figure for the realm from which souls emerge and to which they return. Khayyam's eye moves through three tenses of the dead at once.

lines: تا چند اسیر عقل هرروزه شویم
در دهر چه صد ساله چه یک روزه شویم
در ده تو بکاسه می از آن پیش که ما
در کارگه کوزه گران کوزه شویم
quatrains.source_title: تا چند اسیر عقل هرروزه شویم
literal: How long will we be captives of our daily reasoning?
What is it in this world, whether we live a hundred years or a day?
Pour the wine into the cup, before we ourselves
become pots in the potter's workshop.
poetic: How long must we stay hostage to mere reason?
A hundred years, one day — what's the difference here?
Pour the cup full, and quickly, while we may:
we too will soon be clay the potter shapes.
quatrains.note: A direct statement of the pot-and-potter motif that runs through the Kuza-nama. FitzGerald picks up the "drink before you become a jug" logic in "Then to this earthen Bowl did I adjourn" (FG 1st XXXIV / 5th XXXV).

lines: چون نیست مقام ما در این دهر مُقیم
پس بی می و معشوق خطائی است عظیم
تا کی ز قدیم و محدث امّیدم و بیم
چون من برفتم جهان چه محدث چه قدیم
quatrains.source_title: چون نیست مقام ما در این دهر مقیم
literal: Since our stay in this world is not lasting,
to go without wine and the beloved is a great mistake.
How long, between the Eternal and the Originated, shall I hope and fear?
Once I am gone, what is it to me — originated or eternal?
poetic: Since nothing fixes us in this short hour,
to sit here wineless, loveless, is pure loss.
Why should I dread what's made, and hope what's uncreated?
Once I am gone, the whole debate is dust.
quatrains.note: Qadim (pre-eternal) and muhdath (temporal, contingent) are the cornerstone terms of medieval kalam theology — the argument about whether the world, or the Qur'an, is created or uncreated. Khayyam brushes the whole edifice aside.

lines: خورشید بگل نهفت می نتوانم
و اسرار زمانه گفت می نتوانم
از بحر تفکّرم برآورد خِرَد
دُرّی که ز بیم سفت می‌نتوانم
quatrains.source_title: خورشید بگل نهفت می نتوانم
literal: I cannot hide the sun under clay,
nor can I speak out the secrets of time.
From the sea of my thought, reason has fished up
a pearl that, for fear, I cannot bore through.
poetic: I cannot smother the sun under a lump of clay;
I cannot say the secret the ages guard.
Out of my thought's deep water, reason pulls a pearl
that I lack courage to pierce and string.
quatrains.note: Boring (softan) a pearl is the Persian figure for uttering or publishing a truth. Khayyam hints at heterodox conclusions he dares not speak — a defensive gesture also read by the Sufis as mystical reticence.

lines: دشمن بغلط گفت که من فلسفیم
ایزد داند که آنچه او گفت نیم
لیکن چو درین غم آشیان آمده‌ام
آخر کم از آنکه من بدانم که کیم
quatrains.source_title: دشمن بغلط گفت که من فلسفیم
literal: My enemy has wrongly called me a philosopher;
God knows I am not what he has said.
But since I have come into this nest of sorrow,
at the least I ought to know who I am.
poetic: My enemies have named me philosopher — falsely;
God knows I am no such thing as they declare.
Yet, fallen as I am into this nest of grief,
I ought at least to learn what I am here.
quatrains.note: Kha­y­yam was publicly accused of falsafa (Greek-influenced rationalism), a charge that could be lethal in twelfth-century Nishapur. The tone is part disavowal, part sardonic pride: even if not a philosopher, he won't refuse to examine himself.

lines: مائیم که اصل شادی و کانِ غمیم
سرمایهٔ دادیم و نهادِ ستمیم
پستیم و بلندیم و کمالیم و کمیم
آئینهٔ زنگ خورده و جام جمیم
quatrains.source_title: مائیم که اصل شادی و کان غمیم
literal: We are the root of joy and the mine of grief;
we are the capital of justice and the substance of cruelty.
We are the low and the high, the perfect and the lacking;
we are the rusted mirror and the cup of Jamshid.
poetic: We are the source of joy, the mine of sorrow;
the sum of justice, and the frame of wrong.
We are the high and low, the full and empty —
the tarnished looking-glass, and Jamshid's cup.
quatrains.note: The jam-e Jam (Jamshid's wine-cup) is a mirror-cup in which the whole cosmos appears; the rusted mirror is its fallen counterpart. Khayyam claims both for the human self. Note: trailing line trimmed to four in literal.

lines: من می نه ز بهر تنگدستی نخورم
یا از غم رسوائی و مستی نخورم
من می ز برای خوشدلی میخوردم
اکنون که تو بر دلم نشستی نخورم
quatrains.source_title: من می نه ز بهر تنگدستی نخورم
literal: I do not drink wine out of poverty,
nor out of fear of scandal and drunkenness;
I used to drink wine to lift my heart —
now that you have lodged in my heart, I do not.
poetic: I do not drink from want, nor in defiance;
not to shrug off the scandal of a drunk.
I used to drink to cheer my heart — and now,
since you have set up house there, I don't need to.
quatrains.note: A rare love-poem where the beloved's presence is imagined as replacing wine itself — the drunk motive changes once the heart is already drunk.

lines: من بی می ناب زیستن نتوانم
بی باده کشید بار تن نتوانم
من بندهٔ آن دَمَم که ساقی گوید
یک جام دگر بگیر و من نتوانم
quatrains.source_title: من بی می ناب زیستن نتوانم
literal: I cannot live without pure wine;
without the grape I cannot carry the body's burden.
I am the slave of that moment when the cup-bearer says,
"Take one more cup," and I cannot.
poetic: Without unmixed wine, I cannot stay alive;
without the grape I cannot bear this flesh.
I live for the moment when the saki says,
"One more cup —" and at last I cannot take it.
quatrains.note: A wry inversion: the best moment is not the pour but the point of defeated capacity — the body reaching its ceiling. Saki (cup-bearer) is the beloved's recurring role in Persian bacchic verse.

lines: هر یک چندی یکی برآید که منم
با نعمت و با سیم و زر آید که منم
چون کارک او نظام گیرد روزی
ناگه اجل از کمین درآید که منم
quatrains.source_title: هر یک چندی یکی برآید که منم
literal: Every little while, someone steps up saying "It is I!" —
arriving with riches, silver, and gold, saying "It is I!"
When his small affairs are just coming into order,
suddenly death springs from ambush and says "It is I!"
poetic: Each little while someone comes forward — "Look — it's me!" —
with gold and silver, wealth, and cries "It's me!"
And just as his small business falls in place,
Death springs out of ambush, and says, "It's me."
quatrains.note: The three-fold "I am" builds to Death's punch-line. The ajal-az-kamin (death from ambush) trope is standard in Persian ethical poetry; Khayyam compresses the whole plot of human vanity into four beats.

lines: یک چند بکودکی باُستاد شدیم
یک چند باُستادی خود شاد شدیم
پایان سخن شنو که ما را چه رسید
از خاک درآمدیم و بر باد شدیم
quatrains.source_title: یک چند بکودکی باستاد شدیم
literal: For a while in boyhood we studied under a master;
for a while in our mastership we were pleased with ourselves.
Hear the end of the matter — what came of us:
we came out of the dust, and we went away on the wind.
poetic: A while as boys we studied at a master's feet,
a while as masters we were pleased with ourselves.
Hear the end of the story, what came of us:
we rose out of dust, and we left on the wind.
quatrains.note: Line 4's "came from dust, went on the wind" (az khak bar amadim o bar bad shodim) is one of Khayyam's most famous closing couplets. FitzGerald glosses it as "I came like Water, and like Wind I go" in FG 1st/5th 28.

lines: یک روز ز بند عالم آزاد نیم
یکدم زدن از وجود خود شاد نیم
شاگردی روزگار کردم بسیار
در کار جهان هنوز اُستاد نیم
quatrains.source_title: یک روز ز بند عالم آزاد نیم
literal: Not for a day am I free from the world's chains;
not for a breath am I pleased with my own existence.
I've been a long apprentice to time,
and in the work of the world I am still no master.
poetic: Not one day do I slip the world's rope loose;
not one breath does existence give me joy.
Long have I served my apprenticeship to time,
and still — in this world's craft — I am no master.
quatrains.note: The wordplay turns on ostad, which is both a schoolmaster and a master-craftsman; the quatrain before this (#134) set it up. Khayyam rejects the Sufi's claim to spiritual attainment.

lines: از دی که گذشت هیچ ازو یاد مکن
فردا که نیامده است فریاد مکن
بر نامَده و گذشته بنیاد مکن
حالی خوش باش و عمر بر باد مکن
quatrains.source_title: از دی که گذشت هیچ ازو یاد مکن
literal: Of yesterday that has gone, keep no memory;
of tomorrow that has not come, raise no outcry.
Build nothing on the not-yet or the already-gone;
be glad in the moment, and don't give your life to the wind.
poetic: Of yesterday that's gone, keep no account;
of tomorrow unborn, raise no complaint.
Build nothing on the vanished or unarrived —
take this moment's joy, and don't waste your breath.
quatrains.note: A crystalline statement of Khayyam's Epicurean present-mindedness. FG's LIV/54 ("Waste not your Hour, nor in the vain pursuit of This and That") carries similar force; the closer match is FG 1st XXXVII / 5th 37 ("Unborn TOMORROW and dead YESTERDAY").

lines: ای دیده اگر کور نهٔ گور ببین
وین عالم پُر فتنه و پر شور ببین
شاهان و سران و سروران زیر گلَند
روهای چو مه در دهن مور ببین
quatrains.source_title: ای دیده اگر کور نه گور ببین
literal: O eye, if you are not blind, look at the grave;
look at this world full of unrest and turmoil.
Kings and chiefs and lords are under the soil;
see moon-like faces inside the mouths of ants.
poetic: Eye, if you are not blind, go look at the grave;
look at this world churning with riot and grief.
Kings and princes and lords lie under the clay —
faces like moons, now inside the mouths of ants.
quatrains.note: The image of the ant crawling into a royal mouth is starker than FG ever allowed himself; cf. FG's "They say the Lion and the Lizard keep the Courts where Jamshyd gloried" (XVIII/18) for the milder equivalent.

lines: برخیز و مخور غم جهانِ گذران
بنشین و دَمی بشادمانی گذران
در طبع جهان اگر وفائی بودی
نوبت بتو خود نیامدی از دگران
quatrains.source_title: برخیز و مخور غم جهان گذران
literal: Get up, and do not grieve over this passing world;
sit a while, and pass the time in joy.
If there were any loyalty in the world's disposition,
your own turn would never have come from others.
poetic: Up, and leave off grieving for this passing world;
sit down a little while and pass the hour in joy.
If nature kept its word with anyone,
your turn would never have come down from the others.
quatrains.note: The mordant logic: if the world kept faith, the dead would still be here — and you would not yet have a chance at the table. The argument makes a virtue of the broken promise.

lines: چون حاصل آدمی در این شورستان
جز خوردن غصّه نیست تا کَندنِ جان
خرّم دل آنکه زین جهان زود برفت
و آسوده کسیکه خود نیامد بجهان
quatrains.source_title: چون حاصل آدمی در این شورستان
literal: Since what man gets in this salt-waste
is nothing but eating sorrow until he tears out his soul,
happy is the heart that left this world early,
and at ease whoever never came into the world at all.
poetic: All that a man gathers in this salt-waste world
is grief swallowed down, until the soul is wrenched away.
Happy the heart that quit this place in time,
and lucky he who never came here at all.
quatrains.note: Shurestan (salt-flat) frames the world as an uninhabitable waste. The conclusion — that non-existence beats existence — echoes Sophocles' "best not to be born" and was a provocation that earned Khayyam accusations of heresy.

lines: رفتم که درین منزل بیداد بدن
در دست نخواهد بجز از باد بدن
آنرا باید بمرگ من شاد بدن
کز دست اجل تواند آزاد بدن
quatrains.source_title: رفتم که درین منزل بیداد بدن
literal: I have come, so that in this unjust inn
nothing remains in my hand but wind.
One ought to be glad of my death —
since by the hand of death one can be set free.
poetic: I came into this lodging-house of wrongs
to end with nothing but fistfuls of wind.
Then let my death be matter for rejoicing —
only death's hand can set a soul at liberty.
quatrains.note: Line 2 wordplay on bad (wind / emptiness) — the classic Persian image for futility. A Stoic or even proto-Buddhist note; contrast the later Sufi reading of "freedom" as fana (annihilation in God).

lines: رندی دیدم نشسته بر خنگ زمین
نه کفر و نه اسلام و نه دنیا و نه دین
نه حقّ نه حقیقت نه شریعت نه یقین
اندر دو جهان کرا بود زهرهٔ این
quatrains.source_title: رندی دیدم نشسته بر خنگ زمین
literal: I saw a rogue sitting on the earth's grey steed —
neither heresy, nor Islam, nor world, nor faith;
neither Truth, nor Reality, nor Law, nor certainty.
In the two worlds, who would dare such a stance?
poetic: I saw a rogue astride the horse of earth:
no Islam and no heresy, no world and no faith,
no Truth, no Reality, no Law, no certainty.
Who in the two worlds has the nerve for that?
quatrains.note: The rind (libertine / free-spirit) is Khayyam's and Hafez's highest human type: one who has refused every available category. The cascade of nafi (negations) lists the four pairs of theological alignment: kufr/islam, donya/din, haqq/haqiqat, shari'at/yaqin.

lines: قانع بیک استخوان چو کرکس بودن
به زانکه طفیل خوانِ ناکس بودن
با نان جوینِ خویش حقّا که به است
کالوده بپالوده هر خَس بودن
quatrains.source_title: قانع بیک استخوان چو کرکس بودن
literal: To be content, like the vulture, with a single bone,
is better than to be a parasite at the table of a base man.
Honestly, eating one's own barley bread
is better than being smeared with another's dainties.
poetic: Better to gnaw one bone, like the vulture,
than cringe at the table of some contemptible host.
I swear, a crust of my own barley bread
beats being sticky with another man's sweets.
quatrains.note: A cynic's plain proverb, unusual among the quatrains for addressing economic dependence rather than metaphysics. The vulture (kargas) was an emblem of self-sufficient ugliness in Persian ethical verse.

lines: قومی متفکّرند اندر رهِ دین
قومی بگمان فتاده در راه یقین
میترسم از آنکه بانگ آید روزی
کای بیخبران راه نه آنست و نه این
quatrains.source_title: قومی متفکرند اندر ره دین
literal: A group walks thoughtful on the road of religion;
a group has fallen into conjecture on the road of certainty.
I fear that one day the call will come:
"O fools, the road is neither that one nor this."
poetic: One party walks pondering, on the road of creed;
one party keeps guessing, lost along the road of proof.
I fear one day the herald's cry will come:
"You fools — the road is neither that, nor this."
quatrains.note: This is the source quatrain for FitzGerald's "Fools! your Reward is neither Here nor There" (FG 1st XXIV / 5th 25). Strong match — the muezzin's cry becomes a voice of cosmic disabusal.

lines: گاوی است در آسمان و نامش پروین
یک گاو دگر نهفته در زیر زمین
چشم خِرَدَت باز کن از روی یقین
زیر و زبر دو گاو مشتی خر بین
quatrains.source_title: گاوی است در آسمان و نامش پروین
literal: In the sky is a bull, and its name is the Pleiades;
another bull lies hidden beneath the earth.
Open the eye of reason with the eye of certainty:
under and above those two bulls is a handful of donkeys.
poetic: Up in the sky there is a bull, named Pleiades;
another bull lies hidden beneath the ground.
Open your eye of reason, and look squarely:
between those bulls above and below are a crowd of asses.
quatrains.note: Medieval cosmology placed a celestial bull (Taurus / Parvin) in the sky and a supporting bull under the earth; the middle is humanity — whom Khayyam calls "asses." The pun is brutal: the cosmos is bull above, bull below, fools in between.

lines: گر بر فلکم دست بُدی چون یزدان
برداشتمی من این فلک را ز میان
وز نو فلکی دگر چنان ساختمی
کازاده بکام دل رسیدی آسان
quatrains.source_title: گر بر فلکم دست بدی چون یزدان
literal: If over the heavens I had a hand, like Yazdan,
I would lift this heaven out of the way;
and from scratch I would build another heaven, such a one
that a free man would reach the desire of his heart with ease.
poetic: If I had power over the sky, as God has,
I'd take this heaven and lift it clean away —
and build another from the ground, such that
a free man would get his heart's desire with ease.
quatrains.note: This is the direct source for FitzGerald's most quoted stanza: "Ah, Love! could thou and I with Fate conspire / To grasp this sorry Scheme of Things entire, / Would not we shatter it to bits — and then / Re-mould it nearer to the Heart's Desire!" (FG 1st LXXIII / 5th 99).

lines: مشنو سخن از زمانه ساز آمدگان
می‌خواه مروّق بطراز آمدگان
رفتند یکان یکان فراز آمدگان
کس می ندهد نشان ز بازآمدگان
quatrains.source_title: مشنو سخن از زمانه ساز آمدگان
literal: Don't listen to the talk of those who have come with time's harmony;
ask for clear wine, polished, from those now arrived.
They have gone one by one, those who came up.
No one gives a sign of those who came back.
poetic: Don't heed the words of men set to the world's tune;
ask for the clear, strained wine that the new-come bring.
One by one they have gone, who came up before us;
and of the returning — no one gives any news.
quatrains.note: The fourth line (kas mi nadahad neshan ze bazamadagan) is a direct antecedent of FG's "Not one returns to tell us of the Road" (5th 64) — a much-translated line also quoted by Heron-Allen.

lines: می خوردن و گِردِ نیکوان گردیدن
به زانکه بزرق زاهدی ورزیدن
گر عاشق و مست دوزخی خواهد بود
پس روی بهشت کس نخواهد دیدن
quatrains.source_title: می خوردن و گرد نیکوان گردیدن
literal: Drinking wine and circling among beautiful people
is better than practicing ascetic hypocrisy.
If the lover and the drunk are to be damned,
then no one will ever see the face of paradise.
poetic: Better to drink and keep close to beauty
than work up a sham of pious abstinence.
If lover and drunk are bound for hell,
then no one living will see paradise at all.
quatrains.note: Zarq-e zahedi (hypocritical asceticism) is Khayyam's chief target throughout the Rubaiyat. The rhetoric is classic: if the sincere drunkard is hellbound, heaven empties of human company.

lines: نتوان دل شاد را بغم فرسودن
وقت خوش خود بسنگ محنت سودن
کس غیب چه داند که چه خواهد بودن
می باید و معشوق و بکام آسودن
quatrains.source_title: نتوان دل شاد را بغم فرسودن
literal: One cannot wear down a glad heart with grief,
nor rub one's pleasant hour against the whetstone of suffering.
No one knows the unseen — what is to come.
What's needed is wine, a beloved, and ease at one's desire.
poetic: You cannot grind a cheerful heart down with grief,
nor wear your bright hour on the whetstone of pain.
Nobody knows what's hidden, what's still to come.
The need is simple: wine, a beloved, ease.
quatrains.note: A compact statement of Khayyam's ethics — not indulgence for its own sake, but refusal to pre-pay grief on uncertain debts. "Wine, beloved, ease" is the Epicurean triad.

lines: آن قصر که بر چرخ همی زد پهلو
بر درگَهِ او شهان نهادندی رو
دیدیم که بر کنگره‌اش فاختهٔ
بنشسته همی گفت که کو کو کو کو
quatrains.source_title: آن قصر که بر چرخ همی زد پهلو
literal: That palace which once stood shoulder to shoulder with the sky,
at whose threshold kings pressed their faces to the dust —
we saw on its battlement a ringdove,
sitting and saying, "Where? Where? Where? Where?"
poetic: That palace that once jostled shoulders with the sky,
where kings laid their foreheads on the dust of the sill —
we saw upon its battlement a lonely ringdove,
perched and calling, "Where? Where? Where? Where?"
quatrains.note: FitzGerald included this quatrain verbatim as an extra stanza in his notes to the 5th edition. The ringdove's "ku ku ku ku" ("Where?" in Persian) is the Pehlevi call he mentions; see the note at FG stanza XVIII on Bahram Gur.

lines: از آمدن و رفتن ما سودی کو
وز تار امید عمر ما پودی کو
چندین سر و پای نازنینانِ جهان
میسوزد و خاک میشود دودی کو
quatrains.source_title: از آمدن و رفتن ما سودی کو
literal: Of our coming and going, where is the gain?
And of the thread of life's hope, where is the weave?
So many heads and feet of the earth's darlings
burn down and turn to dust — but where is the smoke?
poetic: Our coming and our going — where's the gain?
On life's hope-loom, what warp is actually strung?
So many lovely heads and feet of earth
burn down to dust — and where is the smoke of it all?
quatrains.note: The accounting image runs through three registers: profit (sud), weave (pud), and smoke (dud) — a single rhyme in Persian. Nothing visible remains; the suggestion borders on material atheism.

lines: از تن چو برفت جانِ پاکِ من و تو
خشتی دو نهند بر مغاک من و تو
وانگاه برای خشت گورِ دگران
در کالبدی کشند خاک من و تو
quatrains.source_title: از تن چو برفت جان پاک من و تو
literal: When the pure soul has departed from the body of you and me,
they will lay two bricks over the pit of you and me.
And then, to brick up graves for other people,
they will mix into the mould the dust of you and me.
poetic: When the clean soul has parted from your body and mine,
they'll lay two bricks above the hollow of us both.
And then — to shape the bricks of other graves —
they'll knead your dust and mine into the mould.
quatrains.note: The pot-and-potter theme extended to masonry: our dust is conscripted into the infrastructure of other burials. Relates to FG 1st XXXVI / 5th 37 (the potter thumping wet clay) and the whole Kuza-nama.

lines: می خور که فلک بهر هلاکِ من و تو
قصدی دارد بجانِ پاکِ من و تو
در سبزه نشین و میِ روشن میخور
کاین سبزه بسی دَمَد ز خاکِ من و تو
quatrains.source_title: می خور که فلک بهر هلاک من و تو
literal: Drink wine, for the wheel of heaven aims at the ruin of you and me,
it has a design on the pure soul of you and me.
Sit on the green grass, and drink bright wine,
for soon this grass will sprout up from the dust of you and me.
poetic: Drink — heaven is plotting the wreck of you and me;
it has its eye on the clean soul of both of us.
Sit on the green, and drink the wine that shines,
for soon enough this grass will grow from our dust.
quatrains.note: Direct source for FG's "This reviving Herb whose tender Green / Fledges the River-Lip on which we lean — / Ah, lean upon it lightly! for who knows / From what once lovely Lip it springs unseen!" (FG 1st XIX / 5th 20).

lines: از هرچه بجز میَ است کوتاهی به
می هم ز کف بُتان خرگاهی به
مستیّ و قلندری و گمراهی به
یک جرعهٔ می ز ماه تا ماهی به
quatrains.source_title: از هرچه بجز می است کوتاهی به
literal: From all but wine, short measure is better;
and wine is best from the hand of tent-dwelling idols.
Drunkenness and the qalandar's life and going astray — all better;
one sip of wine, from moon to fish, is better.
poetic: Of all things save wine, less of it is better;
and even wine is best from a tent-girl's hand.
Drunkenness, the wanderer's way, the losing of the road —
one gulp of wine from moon to fish is best.
quatrains.note: "From moon to fish" (ze mah ta mahi) is Persian for the full vertical span of the cosmos — fish holds up the earth, moon is the first sphere. The qalandar is the antinomian dervish who rejects all conventional piety.

lines: بنگر ز صبا دامنِ گُل چاک شده
بلبل ز جمال گُل طربناک شده
در سایهٔ گُل نشین که بسیار این گُل
در خاک فرو ریزد و ما خاک شده
quatrains.source_title: بنگر ز صبا دامن گل چاک شده
literal: Look — from the dawn breeze, the skirt of the rose has been torn;
the nightingale has grown delirious from the rose's beauty.
Sit in the rose's shade, for again and again this rose
will fall into the dust, and we — we will have gone to dust.
poetic: Look — the dawn wind has split the rose's skirt;
the nightingale goes giddy with her beauty.
Sit in the rose's shade. Again, again,
this rose will drop to earth — and we to dust.
quatrains.note: The rose (gol) and the nightingale (bolbol) are the inseparable lovers of Persian lyric. FG echoes this pair in 5th 6 and 96. The cycle of returns — this rose, that rose, all ending in dust — is pure Khayyam.

lines: تا کی غم آن خورم که دارم یا نه
وین عمر بخوشدلی گذارم یا نه
پُر کن قدح باده که معلومم نیست
کایندم که فرو برم بر آرم یا نه
quatrains.source_title: تا کی غم آن خورم که دارم یا نه
literal: How long shall I grieve whether I have or I don't,
and whether I pass this life in cheer or not?
Fill the cup with wine — for it is not certain
that this breath I take in, I'll live to let back out.
poetic: How long must I fret over having, or not having?
Whether this life is passed in joy — or otherwise?
Fill the cup. For I am not quite sure
that the breath I'm drawing in, I'll exhale again.
quatrains.note: Compresses the whole Khayyam argument into the span of a single breath. Related in spirit to FG's LXXIV/74 "Drink! for you not know whence you came."

lines: یک جرعه میِ کهن ملکی نو به
وز هرچه نه می طریق بیرون شو به
در دست به از تخت فریدون صدبار
خشتِ سر خم ز مُلک کیخسرو به
quatrains.source_title: یک جرعه می کهن ملکی نو به
literal: One sip of old wine is better than a new kingdom;
everything but wine — it is better to walk away from.
The jar's mouth-shard is a hundred times better than Faridun's throne;
and better than Kay Khosrow's kingdom is the clay lip of the jug.
poetic: One sip of old wine beats a brand-new kingdom;
go past everything that isn't wine — and go quick.
A wine-jar's broken lip is a hundred times
better than the throne of Faridun, the crown of Kay Khosrow.
quatrains.note: Faridun and Kay Khosrow are Shahnameh kings of the mythic Pishdadian and Kayanian dynasties — the emblems of absolute sovereignty. Khayyam undercuts them with a piece of pottery. FG folds this move into his "take the Cash" arguments (13/12).

lines: آن مایه ز دنیا که خوری یا پوشی
معذوری اگر در طلبش میکوشی
باقی همه رایگان نیرزد هشدار
تا عمر گرانبها بدان نفروشی
quatrains.source_title: آن مایه ز دنیا که خوری یا پوشی
literal: That much of the world — what you eat, or what you wear —
you are excused if you struggle after it.
All the rest is worthless. Pay attention:
do not sell your precious life for it.
poetic: What little of the world you'll eat, or wear —
struggle for that, and you'll be forgiven the struggle.
All the rest is worth nothing. Pay attention:
do not trade your priceless life for any of it.
quatrains.note: A plain-prose ethics — one of the quatrains in which Khayyam sounds less Epicurean than ascetic. Persian razdan ("cheap / worthless") puns against the precious life (omr-e geran-baha) in line 4.

lines: از آمدنِ بهار و از رفتن دی
اوراق وجود ما همی گردد طی
می خور مخور اندوه که فرمود حکیم
غمهای جهان چو زهر و تریاقش می
quatrains.source_title: از آمدن بهار و از رفتن دی
literal: With spring's coming and winter's going,
the pages of our existence keep folding up.
Drink wine, and do not take on grief, for the sage has said:
the griefs of the world are like poison — and its antidote is wine.
poetic: With spring arriving and winter going away,
the leaves of our existence fold themselves up one by one.
Drink, and do not carry grief — the sage has said:
the world's sorrows are poison — wine is the cure.
quatrains.note: Cf. FG 1st / 5th 8 ("The Leaves of Life keep falling one by one") — the shared image of the folding pages of existence. Tariq (antidote) and zahr (poison) pair as a medical couplet.

lines: از کوزه گری کوزه خریدم باری
آن کوزه سخن گفت ز هر اسراری
شاهی بودم که جام زرّینم بود
اکنون شده‌ام کوزهٔ هر خمّاری
quatrains.source_title: از کوزه گری کوزه خریدم باری
literal: I once bought a jug from a potter,
and that jug spoke of every kind of secret.
"I was a king, who had a golden cup;
now I have become the jug of some drunkard."
poetic: One day I bought a jug from a potter's stall;
and every kind of secret came out of that clay.
"I was a king once, who had a cup of gold;
now I am any drunkard's common jar."
quatrains.note: Belongs to the Kuza-nama (Book of Pots) cycle. The speaking jug is FG's LXXXIII–XC / 1st LIX–LXVI — though FG builds a whole Ramazan-tavern scene around the motif rather than this single vignette.

lines: ای آنکه نتیجهٔ چهار و هفتی
وز هفت و چهار دائم اندر تفتی
می خور که هزار بار بیشت گفتم
باز آمدنت نیست چو رفتی رفتی
quatrains.source_title: ای آنکه نتیجه چهار و هفتی
literal: O you, the product of four and seven,
forever in a fever over four and seven —
drink wine, for I have told you a thousand times before:
there is no coming back for you — once gone, you are gone.
poetic: O you, composed of four and seven,
always in a fever about the four and the seven —
drink. I have told you a thousand times before:
there is no coming back for you — once you're gone, you're gone.
quatrains.note: Four elements, seven spheres: the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic cosmos from which the human is compounded. Khayyam shrugs off the whole machinery. Compare FG 5th 64: "Not one returns to tell us of the Road."

lines: ایدل تو باسرار معمّا نرسی
در نکته زیرکان دانا نرسی
این‌جا بمی لعل بهشتی میساز
کآنجا که بهشت است رسی یا نرسی
quatrains.source_title: ایدل تو باسرار معما نرسی
literal: O heart, you will never reach the riddle's secrets,
you will never reach the subtle point of the wise and knowing;
here, with wine and the ruby lip, make your own paradise —
since to that other paradise, who knows whether you'll arrive.
poetic: Heart, you will never solve the riddle's secret;
never catch up with the subtle wit of the wise.
Here, with wine and a ruby lip, build your own paradise —
as for the other one — who knows if you'll arrive.
quatrains.note: The rhetorical pivot: build paradise now, since the promised paradise is speculation. Wine + ruby lip (may-e la'l) is both bacchic and erotic — a standard Khayyam compound figure.

lines: ای دوست حقیقت شنو از من سخنی
با بادهٔ لعل باش و با سیم تنی
کانکس که جهان کرد فراغت دارد
از سبلت چون توئی و ریش چو منی
quatrains.source_title: ای دوست حقیقت شنو از من سخنی
literal: O friend, hear a word of truth from me:
be with ruby wine, and with a body of silver.
The one who made the world is untroubled, without care,
about a moustache like yours or a beard like mine.
poetic: Friend, hear from me a single piece of truth:
keep company with ruby wine and silver skin.
The one who made the world is quite at ease
about your moustache, my friend, or a beard like mine.
quatrains.note: A compact anti-clerical jab. The theological point: the Creator is faragh (at ease, undistracted) and does not audit facial hair or ritual observance. The beard was a chief index of piety.

lines: ای کاش که جای آرمیدن بودی
یا این ره دور را رسیدن بودی
کاش از پی صدهزار سال از دلِ خاک
چون سبزه امید بر دمیدن بودی
quatrains.source_title: ای کاش که جای آرمیدن بودی
literal: If only there were a place to rest at,
or if only there were an end to this long road;
if only, after a hundred thousand years, from the heart of the dust,
like the grass, there were a hope of our rising up again.
poetic: If only there were a resting-place to reach,
or an end to this long road we travel down;
if only — after a hundred thousand years, out of the earth —
like grass, we had some hope of coming up again.
quatrains.note: The conditional mood (ay kash) expresses a wish that is also a doubt. Note the austere position: Khayyam imagines not resurrection but the botanical chance of grass.

lines: بر سنگ زدم دوش سبوی کاشی
سرمست بُدم چو کردم این اوباشی
با من بزبان حال میگفت سبو
من چون تو بُدم تو نیز چون من باشی
quatrains.source_title: بر سنگ زدم دوش سبوی کاشی
literal: Last night, in drunkenness, I struck a glazed jug on a stone;
I was drunk when I did this hooligan act.
The jug said to me, in the language of its condition:
"I was once like you — and you will one day be like me."
poetic: Last night I smashed a glazed jug on a stone;
drunk as I was, I did this hooligan thing.
The jug said to me, plainly, in the tongue of its state:
"I was like you once. You too will be like me."
quatrains.note: Another pot-poem. Man chun to bodam, to niz chun man bashi ("I was like you, you will be like me") is one of the most quoted lines in the Rubaiyat and echoes a medieval Arabic tomb-inscription commonplace. Heron-Allen flagged this as a source for FG's potter-shop stanzas.

lines: بر شاخ امید اگر بری یافتمی
هم رشتهٔ خویش را سری یافتمی
تا چند ز تنگنای زندانِ وجود
ایکاش سوی عدم دری یافتمی
quatrains.source_title: بر شاخ امید اگر بری یافتمی
literal: If I had found fruit on the branch of hope,
I would have caught hold of the thread of my own life.
How long in the narrow prison of existence?
I wish I could find a door out toward non-being.
poetic: If the branch of hope had borne me any fruit,
I would have found an end to my own thread.
How much longer in this narrow cell of being?
I wish I could find a door out into nothing.
quatrains.note: A bleak statement: the tanga-ye vojud (narrow prison of existence) is rare in Khayyam — usually the cell metaphor is claustrophobia; here it reaches toward escape. Suggests a Schopenhauerian strain long before Schopenhauer.

lines: برگیر پیاله و سبو ای دلجوی
فارغ بنشین بکِشته‌زار و لبِ جوی
بس شخص عزیز را که چرخ بدخوی
صدبار پیاله کرد و صد بار سبوی
quatrains.source_title: برگیر پیاله و سبو ای دلجوی
literal: Heart-seeker, pick up the cup and the jug;
sit easy by the planted field and the edge of the stream.
Many a precious person has the ill-tempered wheel
made into a cup a hundred times, a jug a hundred times.
poetic: Come, heart-seeker — take up the cup and the jug;
sit at ease by the green field, by the brook's edge.
So many lovely people have the surly wheel
turned, a hundred times, into cups and jars.
quatrains.note: A lighter-voiced potter variant, pairing the garden-picnic scene (a standard Khayyam setting) with the grim production pipeline of the heavens. Has echoes of FG's strip-of-herbage (1st X / 5th 11).

lines: پیری دیدم بخانهٔ خمّاری
گفتم نکنی ز رفتگان اخباری
گفتا می خور که همچو ما بسیاری
رفتند و خبر باز نیامد باری
quatrains.source_title: پیری دیدم بخانه خماری
literal: I saw an old man at a wineseller's house;
I said, "Can't you give me news of those who have gone?"
He said, "Drink wine — for many like us
have gone, and no news has come back."
poetic: I saw an old man at the wineshop door;
I said, "Tell me — any word from those who went?"
He answered, "Drink. For many like ourselves
have gone that way, and never sent back word."
quatrains.note: A close match for FG's 5th 64 ("Strange, is it not? that of the myriads who / Before us passed the door of Darkness through, / Not one returns..."). The wineseller-sage is a stock figure of Persian bacchic poetry, part Socratic interlocutor, part tavern-keeper.

lines: تا چند حدیث پنج و چار ای ساقی
مشکل چه یکی چه صد هزار ای ساقی
خاکیم همه چنگ بساز ای ساقی
بادیم همه باده بیار ای ساقی
quatrains.source_title: تا چند حدیث پنج و چار ای ساقی
literal: How long the talk of the five and four, O saki?
Whether one problem or a hundred thousand — what is it, saki?
We are all dust — set up the harp, saki;
we are all wind — bring the wine, saki.
poetic: How long these lectures on the five and four, saki?
One problem or a hundred thousand — what's the difference?
We're all dust — so strike the harp, saki;
we're all wind — so pour the wine, saki.
quatrains.note: Five senses and four elements — the cogs of scholastic psychology. The refrain-style address to the saki, with the anaphora khakim / badim (we are dust / we are wind), is one of the most musically tight in Khayyam.

lines: چندانکه نگاه میکنم هر سوئی
در باغ روان است ز کوثر جوئی
صحرا چو بهشت است ز کوثر کم گوی
بنشین به بهشت با بهشتی روئی
quatrains.source_title: چندانکه نگاه میکنم هر سوئی
literal: However far I look, in any direction,
in the flowing garden runs a stream of Kawthar;
the plain is like paradise — say little of Kawthar;
sit in paradise, with a paradise-faced companion.
poetic: Wherever I look, in any direction at all,
the garden is running with streams of Kawthar.
The plain itself is paradise — spare me the sermons.
Sit here, in paradise — with a paradise-faced friend.
quatrains.note: Kawthar is the river of paradise in Islamic eschatology (Qur'an 108). Khayyam relocates it to the spring garden, and the houri to the beloved at hand. Strongly ironic against clerical promises.

lines: خوش باش که پخته‌اند سودای تو دی
فارغ شده‌اند از تمنّای تو دی
قصّه چکنم که بی تقاضای تو دی
دادند قرار فردای تو دی
quatrains.source_title: خوش باش که پخته‌اند سودای تو دی
literal: Be glad, for yesterday they cooked the business of you;
yesterday they were done with all longing for you.
What a tale — without your asking, yesterday
they settled the arrangements for your tomorrow.
poetic: Be at ease: yesterday they finished cooking your story;
yesterday they were done with longing for you.
What a case — without your asking, yesterday
they set the terms of your tomorrow, for good.
quatrains.note: The perfect tense throughout makes the point: every detail of your fate is already settled. A direct statement of qaza-o-qadar (Islamic predestination), but in a tone close to fatigue, not piety.

lines: در کارگه کوزه‌گری کردم رای
در پایهٔ چرخ دیدم اُستاد بپای
میکرد دلیر کوزه را دسته و سر
از کلّه پادشاه و از دست گدای
quatrains.source_title: در کارگه کوزه‌گری کردم رای
literal: I went to the potter's workshop, with thought on my mind;
at the foot of the wheel I saw the master at work.
He was boldly making a jug's handle and mouth
from a king's skull and a beggar's hand.
poetic: I went into the potter's shop, with thinking in my head;
at the foot of the wheel the master stood at work.
Boldly he was making handles and jar-mouths
from the skulls of kings, and the hands of beggars.
quatrains.note: A key source-quatrain for the whole Kuza-nama of FitzGerald (FG 1st LIX–LXVI / 5th LXXXII–XC). The compression here — king's skull, beggar's hand, one jug — is more brutal than FG's more loquacious English pots.

lines: در گوش دلم گفت فلک پنهانی
حکمی که قضا بود ز من میدانی
در گردش خویش اگر مرا دست بدی
خود را برهاندمی ز سرگردانی
quatrains.source_title: در گوش دلم گفت فلک پنهانی
literal: The sky whispered a secret into my heart's ear:
"The decrees that come down as fate — those, you know, come from me.
In my own turning, if I had a hand,
I would have freed myself long ago from all this dizziness."
poetic: The wheel of heaven whispered, secretly, to me:
"These decrees that fall as fate — you know, I pass them down.
But in my own spinning, had I any hand,
I would long have saved myself from all this dizziness."
quatrains.note: The sky admits that it is as driven as we are. Source (with others) for FG's 5th 72: "And that inverted Bowl they call the Sky... As impotently moves as you or I."

lines: زان کوزهٔ می که نیست در وی ضرری
پُر کن قدحی بخور بمن ده دگری
زان پیشتر ای صنم که در رهگذری
خاکِ من و تو کوزه کند کوزه‌گری
quatrains.source_title: زان کوزه می که نیست در وی ضرری
literal: From that wine-jug, the one that brings no harm,
fill a cup, drink, and give another to me;
before — O idol — in some roadway or other,
the potter makes jugs out of the dust of you and me.
poetic: From that wine-jar, the one that does no one harm,
fill a cup, drink it down, and pass another to me;
before — my idol — some day at some crossroads,
the potter turns us, you and me, to jugs.
quatrains.note: Another variant of the "drink before you're clay" logic. Sanam (idol) is a term of affection for the beloved throughout Persian bacchic verse, not literal idolatry.

lines: گر آمدنم بخود بُدی نامدمی
ور نیز شدن بمن بُدی کی شدمی
به زان نبُدی که اندر این دیر خراب
نه آمدمی نه شدمی نه بُدمی
quatrains.source_title: گر آمدنم بخود بدی نامدمی
literal: If my coming had been up to me, I would not have come;
if, too, my going had been up to me, when would I have gone?
Better than this would be — that in this ruined inn —
I had neither come, nor gone, nor been at all.
poetic: Had my coming been my choice, I would not have come;
had going been my choice, when would I have gone?
Better than this — that, in this broken inn —
I had not come, nor gone, nor ever been.
quatrains.note: The triple na (neither–nor–nor) at line 4 is one of the most shocking closings in the Rubaiyat. The complaint is against consent: none of us signed the contract of being. Ali Dashti called this the clearest kufri (infidel) quatrain.

lines: گر دست دهد ز مغز گندم نانی
وز می دو منی ز گوسفندی رانی
با لاله رخیّ و گوشهٔ بُستانی
عیشی بود آن نه حدّ هر سلطانی
quatrains.source_title: گر دست دهد ز مغز گندم نانی
literal: If a fellow has the luck — a loaf of wheat bread,
and two liters of wine, and the flank of a sheep,
with a tulip-cheeked beloved in a corner of the garden —
that would be a pleasure above the reach of any sultan.
poetic: If a man can come by a loaf of good wheat bread,
two measures of wine, and a sheep's leg,
with a tulip-cheeked companion in a corner of the garden —
that is a pleasure no sultan ever bought.
quatrains.note: This is the closest known Persian source for FitzGerald's "A Book of Verses underneath the Bough, / A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread — and Thou" (FG 1st XI / 5th 12). FG substitutes verses for the sheep's leg — a Victorian literary preference.

lines: گر کار فلک بعدل سنجیده بُدی
احوال فلک جمله پسندیده بُدی
ور عدل بُدی بکارها در گردون
کی خاطر اهل فضل رنجیده بُدی
quatrains.source_title: گر کار فلک بعدل سنجیده بدی
literal: If the work of the heavens had been weighed with justice,
all the conditions of the heavens would be admirable.
If there were justice in the dealings of the wheel,
when would men of excellence ever have been aggrieved?
poetic: If heaven's work were weighed on the scale of justice,
its business would all be admirable and right.
If there were any justice in the wheel's affairs,
when would men of merit ever have been grieved?
quatrains.note: A plain complaint against the cosmos: the just world hypothesis is checked by the evidence and found false. The ahl-e fazl (people of excellence) are suffering; therefore the wheel is not just.

lines: هان کوزه گرا بپای اگر هشیاری
تا چند کنی بر گل مردم خواری
انگشت فریدون و کفِ کیخسرو
بر چرخ نهادهٔ چه می‌پنداری
quatrains.source_title: هان کوزه گرا بپای اگر هشیاری
literal: Hey, potter, watch your feet, if you're sober;
how long will you go on trampling human clay?
The finger of Faridun, the palm of Kay Khosrow,
you have put on your wheel — what are you thinking?
poetic: Potter, watch where you step — if you still have your wits;
how long will you go on trampling the dust of men?
The finger of Faridun, the palm of Kay Khosrow,
you have thrown on your wheel — what are you thinking?
quatrains.note: Close companion to #171 and #159 — the Kuza-nama cycle's ethical voice: the potter treads on royal dust without knowing it. Compare FG's LXXXIV/84 ("My substance of the common Earth was ta'en").

lines: هنگام صبوح ای صنم فرّخ پی
برساز ترانهٔ و پیش آور می
کافکند بخاک صد هزاران جم و کی
این آمدن تیر مه و رفتن دی
quatrains.source_title: هنگام صبوح ای صنم فرّخ پی
literal: At the hour of the morning cup, O my lucky-footed idol,
set the tune and bring forward the wine;
for into the dust it has thrown a hundred thousand Jamshids and Kays —
this coming of Tir month, this going of Dey.
poetic: At the hour of the dawn-cup, my lucky-footed love,
strike up the tune, and bring the wine around;
a hundred thousand Jamshids and Kay kings it has laid in the dust —
this coming of midsummer, this passing of winter.
quatrains.note: Tir (June–July) and Dey (December–January) are Persian solar months; their revolution has already buried Jamshid and the Kayanian dynasty. A close cousin to FG's 5th 9 ("And this first Summer Month that brings the Rose / Shall take Jamshyd and Kaikobad away").
